course.title: Qual App Comp Political Analysis
course.description: This is an advanced seminar that introduces majors to debates and methods in qualitative approaches to analyzing and explaining political phenomena. We will focus on what the comparative method allows us to know about politics, and study how comparativists pose and answer research questions and approach causality, through case studies, comparative historical analysis, process tracing, discourse analysis, and interpretive methods. Readings will pair methods with literatures on topics like democratization, social movements, ethnic conflict, nationalism, and political violence, and students will produce original research plans. Recommended for students planning to write theses in comparative politics.

course.title: The Politics of God
course.description: Why and how does religion continue to exercise political influence in a secular age? This course examines how religion is mobilized in democratic politics, by national and state elites, and by revolutionary and fundamentalist movements in global,comparative case contexts.

course.title: Race in American Politics
course.description: This course examines the centrality of race in American politics. The course examines how racial and ethnic interest groups pursue political power and the relative success of their efforts. Thematically, the course will focus on how these groups interact with strategic political actors working within established political institutions.

course.title: Philosophy of Feminism
course.description: Examines several different theories of feminism, their relation to traditional political theories, and their analyses of the causes and solutions to women's oppression. The course considers as well specific moral and political issues relevant to feminism: abortion, motherhood, reproductive technologies, and pornography. The course includes attending six writing workshops at a local women's prison, Tuesday evenings 4:30-9:00pm.

course.title: Complex Analysis
course.description: The beautiful and elegant theorems which are encountered in complex analysis form a cornerstone of mathematics.  In this course we will apply familiar concepts such as line integrals and differentiability to complex-valued functions. We will investigate the Cauchy-Riemann equations, and study holomorphic and meromorphic functions via Taylor and Laurent series. Cauchy's theorem and integral formula along with the calculus of residues will be featured. We will also introduce conformal mappings and harmonic functions. Prerequisite:  Math 60.  Math 101 or 131 are recommended.

course.title: Gndr/Tstmny in LatAm & Caribbean
course.description: The course is structured around pathbreaking texts that are life histories of non-elite women or testimonies. Through testimony we will explore problems of theory and analysis addressing feminism, womynism, racial justice, and economic dignity, as well as the queering of revolution in 21st century Latin America and the Caribbean. Today, African and Indigenous gender identities lie at the heart of movements for justice that have won national power. This region of the world with 600 million people has lifted 70 million people out of poverty in recent decades, thanks to the organizing of women such as those whose words we will read and hear in this course.

course.title: Cult Crit Freud Edelman
course.description: This course examines important works of 20th- and 21st-century cultural criticism as a response to the challenges faced by Western societies (world wars, the dismantling of Empire and the process of decolonization, political struggles against various forms of social inequality). The course pays particular attention to the preoccupation with society as a problem for individual (human) freedom, as articulated in writings by Freud, Lévi-Strauss, Fanon, Adorno, Genet, Said, and Edelman. Course meets Social Science general education requirement. Course also offered as HIST124 SC.

course.title: Writing SWANA America
course.description: We explore the writing and lives of Southwest Asians and North Africans in North America. We begin with the continent's first Arabic-language writers, mostly enslaved Muslim West Africans, then move to writing by and about 19th- and early 20th-century immigrants from Lebanon, Armenia, and other parts of West Asia. Finally, we explore SWANA-American literature of the 20th- and 21st centuries, with a particular focus on the complexities of how SWANA-Americans are racialized and how the Iranian Revolution, 9/11, and the ?War on Terror? have reshaped the material realities and Orientalist stereotypes that SWANA-American writers negotiate. Course meets Letters and Race and Ethnic Studies general education requirement.

course.title: Intro to French&Francophone Stds
course.description: This gateway course introduces students to Francophone Studies, a deeply interdisciplinary field informed by approaches from the arts, humanities, and social sciences. Students will acquire a range of conceptual tools and ideas that they will apply through traditional and non-traditional analysis of visual, written, and performative practices of the French-speaking world. Conducted in French. Prerequisite: FREN044 or equivalent.

course.title: Continued Introductory French
course.description: Study of more advanced grammatical structures and syntax. Intensive practice in speaking, reading, and writing. Students taking FREN002 are also required to attend a weekly 45-minute conversation session with a native assistant. Prerequisite: FREN001 or French Placement Test.

course.title: Basic Helping Skills
course.description: Basic Helping Skills is a practical course intended to introduce students to active listening. In the class, we will explore the fundamental listening and responding skills that distill into clinical practice. This will involve in-class and peer-to-peer practice of listening and responding. Students will also be exposed to basic tenants of psychotherapy and the critical microskills used to facilitate therapeutic interactions.

course.title: Psychology and Law
course.description: This course will survey issues in psychology and law including an introduction to the legal system, eyewitness identification, confessions, competence and insanity, jury decision making, victims, and sentencing issues. Basic psychological theory, relevant case law, and methodological issues associated with conducting research in psychology and law will be covered. Prerequisite: Psychology 52.

course.title: Topics: Stereotyping & Prejudice
course.description:
Repeatable for credit with different topics. Prerequisites: Psychology 52, 168, or permission of instructor.

Topic: Stereotyping and Prejudice in Society. This course will begin with a survey of the social psychological literature on stereotyping and prejudice before exploring every-day applications or outcomes of these constructs. Topics may include stereotype threat, implicit stereotyping, motivations to control prejudice, and implications for the legal system, business, politics, media, and schools.

course.title: Clinical Neuropsychology
course.description: This course will study human clinical neuropsychology with an emphasis on clinical disorders, including learning disorders, dementias, and traumatic brain injuries. There will be an emphasis on integrating theory and research related to brain functioning and applying this knowledge to clinical populations. Prerequisite: Psychology 52.

course.title: Languages for Religious Studies
course.description: This course solidifies the basic linguistic principles covered in RLST 195L (or equivalent), develops familiarity with specialized vocabulary, complex sentence structures and ideas, identifies and explains linguistic irregularities, and, where appropriate, notes regional or dialectical variations. Emphasis on reading and translating texts of intermediate-level difficulty. Course has language pre-requisistes.

course.title: Languages for Religious Studies
course.description: This course is designed to familiarize students with specific authors or textual traditions relevant to their projected specialization in graduate school. Emphasis on reading and translating texts of advanced-level difficulty.  Course has language pre-requisistes.

course.title: Languages for Religious Studies
course.description: This course is designed to familiarize students with specific authors or textual traditions relevant to their projected specialization in graduate school. Emphasis on reading and translating texts of advanced-level difficulty.  Course has language pre-requisistes.

course.title: Intensive Introductory Spanish
course.description: Designed for beginning students with some basic knowledge of the language, who are too advanced for Spanish 1, but do not yet qualify for Spanish 33. Students will fulfill in one semester the equivalent of Spanish 1 and 2. This course includes laboratory work and tutorial sessions (times arranged). Prerequisite: Language Placement Test.

course.title: Introduction to Hinduism
course.description: How did the diverse traditions now called Hinduism take shape? This course follows that story from its earliest hymns through its devotional poetry, reading primary sources in translation: the Vedas and Upanishads, Samkhya philosophy, the dharma literature, the Mahabharata and Ramayana, the Puranas, and the poet-saints of the bhakti movements. Throughout the semester, the course asks how these early texts and practices inform Hinduism as it is lived today.

course.title: The Hungry Brain
course.description: This course is an introduction to neuroscience for non-majors that will explore the neurobiology of hunger and food-associated behaviors. This course will cover mechanisms that regulate appetite, food-seeking, food consumption, and energy state in humans from the perspectives of endocrinology, physiology, and the gut-brain axis. Several diseases will be discussed including diabetes, eating disorders (e.g., Anorexia), and Narcolepsy Type I, as well as current and emerging therapeutic interventions, including GLP-1 therapies.

course.title: More-than-Human Worlds
course.description: Across the history of western thought, the idea of ?the Human? has been central to establishing hierarchies of power, access to resources, and what counts as valuable life. Feminist theories of gender and race, nature and culture, vegetality (plant life) and animality, creatures and monsters, cyborgs and androids, and ?more-than-human? worlds have been developed to challenge human exceptionalism and to suggest that intelligence, agency, language, feeling, desire, and will are not solely human features but are integral to the animate earth. In this course, we will read feminist and queer texts that grapple with the ethical, political, and existential implications in the question, ?what is the Human?? We will consider how the answers to that question shape our understandings of what is possible in being a body in relation to other bodies and our sense of which bodies and lives matter. This course fulfills the GWS theory requirement.

course.title: Music of the Spirits
course.description: Music of the Spirits: Hakka, Hawaiian, and Tewa Pueblo Indian. This course will explore three sacred musical cultures: Hakka mountain songs and the Unicorn dance, Hawaiian hula kahiko and auana and Tewa Pueblo ritual dance ceremonies. We will assess how systemic discrimination and exploitation of Asians, Pacific Islanders and Native Americans impacted these musical practices. Readings draw upon writings and interviews by minority scholars speaking about their own cultures, as well as drawing on secondary sources.  Meets Fine Arts general education requirement.

course.title: Print Cultures: Hist and Theory
course.description: This course will introduce students to the history, theory, and practice printmaking in Europe, Asia, and the Americas with emphasis on first-hand analysis of works in the collections held at the Benton Museum of Art at Pomona College and the Williamson Gallery at Scripps College. Students will consider the development of various printmaking techniques, including woodcut, engraving, etching, and lithography. Each semester the course is offered will present a different special topic. Course assignments will be designed to include writing for exhibition texts, development of sample exhibition checklists, artist biographies, and other object-based research.

course.title: Intro American Politics (Honors)
course.description: Introduces the student to the scholarly study of government and politics with special reference to the political principles and constitutional structure of the American system, interpreted in the light of political philosophy, the dynamics of public opinion, interest groups, political parties, and public policy. First and second semester.

course.title: Music in Christian Practice
course.description: Music serves an essential role in Christian worship and devotional practices. This course examines the musical practices in various historical and present-day worship settings ranging from medieval European monasteries and American revival campus to contemporary mainline Protestant churches of various racial and ethnic groups in the United States. This course satisfies the fine arts requirement. This course satisfies the fine arts requirement.

course.title: One-Semester Thesis in Biology
course.description: All students who intend to complete a one-semester thesis should enroll in this course. Students are required both to submit a substantive written thesis - which may involve experimental work, analysis of datasets previously collected by other researchers, or a critical analysis of the literature - and to make a formal presentation. Students register for this course during the semester in which the one-semester thesis is written and due. There is no lab fee for this course.Offered every semester.

course.title: One-Semester Thesis in Physics
course.description: All students who intend to complete a one-semester thesis should enroll in this course. Students are required both to submit a substantive written thesis - which may involve experimental work, analysis of datasets previously collected by other researchers, or a critical analysis of the literature - and to make a formal presentation. Students register for this course during the semester in which the one-semester thesis is written and due. There is no lab fee for this course.

course.title: One-Sem Thesis in Neuroscience
course.description: All students who intend to complete a one-semester thesis should enroll in this course. Students are required both to submit a substantive written thesis, which may involve experimental work, analysis of datasets previously collected by other researchers, or a critical analysis of the literature, and to make a forma presentation. Students register for this course during the semester in which the one-semester thesis is written and due.

course.title: NMR Spectroscopy
course.description: Examines fundamental concepts in nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy including the physical basis of magnetic resonance and one- and two-dimensional techniques for the elucidation of structure and dynamics. The course includes hands-on experience with data collection and analysis. Lecture. One-half course credit. Prerequisites: completion of or concurrent enrollment in Chemistry 117L and 122.

course.title: One-Semester Thesis in Chemistry
course.description: All students who intend to complete a one-semester thesis should enroll in this course. Students are required both to submit a substantive written thesis - which may involve experimental work, analysis of datasets previously collected by other researchers, or a critical analysis of the literature - and to make a formal presentation. Students register for this course during the semester in which the one-semester thesis is written and due.

course.title: Earth History & Evolution
course.description: Earth History & Evolution explores the interactions of life and our dynamic Earth over geologic time. The course introduces key concepts of plate tectonics, geologic time, rock identification, and tracks the evolution and extinctions of life from the simplest single-celled organisms of the ancient Earth to today's diverse floras and faunas.

course.title: Statistics for Neuroscience
course.description: An introduction to data analysis and statistical reasoning for neuroscience. Students will learn how to work with neural and behavioral datasets, visualize and summarize data, build and interpret statistical models, and evaluate the strength of scientific evidence. Emphasis is placed on reproducible research practices using interactive coding notebooks and real experimental data. Course meets Mathematics general education requirement.

course.title: Unveiling the Erotic
course.description: Europe's early 20th century saw rapid social change as cities grew and people of different backgrounds spent increasing time in close proximity. Artists of this period grew more daring in their explorations of the human psyche, depicting transgressive eroticism and sexual subcultures in their works. In this course, we'll study prose texts and films that challenged propriety and portrayed human sexuality more openly. Texts will include novels and films from Germany, Austria, France, and England. Course meets Letters and Gender and Women's Studies general education requirements.

course.title: Arts + Culture Review
course.description: This course is a writing workshop designed to enhance your skills in the journalistic review. Focusing on reviews of food, travel, books, film, music, and art and performance, we'll read reviews from the best practitioners in each area as well as cultural theories of taste and aesthetics and discuss the politics of both. We'll develop our critical palates by doing tast tests and short critiques in class. Finally, we'll talk about the ethics and logistics of reviewing as well as issues of form. Assignments will include reviews in each area and critical responses to the reviews of others.

course.title: Introduction to Podcasting
course.description: In this course, to ground us in the foundations of today's rapid rise in audiobooks and podcasts, we begin with tradition of oral storytelling in ancient Greece and in African and African American traditions. We will then examine a range of approaches to podcasting and the ways in which these approaches connect with and disrupt other forms of argument-driven writing. Students will select a podcast and analyze the way it presents and tells a story about a specific topic, considering both the text and accompanying audio content and sounds. Students will then create and deliver their own podcast episode. This course is an Inside-Out course. Inside-Out courses are regular college courses that are part of the international Inside-Out Prison Exchange Center model that "bring together campus-based college students with incarcerated students for a semester-long course." These courses are slated as "Permission of Instructor Required" so that the faculty members can fully explain the nature of the course and request students to complete an application or interview prior to enrollment. Your peers for this course will include women currently experiencing incarceration in DTLA. You should plan for a buffer of time (1-1.5 hours) before and after class for transportation. You will also need to share information for the clearance process before the semester begins.

course.title: Contemporary Sociological Theory
course.description: Examines some of the more influential and compelling theories, paradigms, and thinkers from within the discipline of sociology since World War Two. Strongly recommended for students considering graduate school.

course.title: Social Networks and Modeling Cli
course.description: This course explores the mathematics of social networks, how to represent them, measure their properties, and model them using probability. We will begin by building a foundation in network theory, then examine patterns observed in real-world networks, and study probabilistic models that capture their structure. In the final portion of the course, we will apply these tools to investigate how network structure can influence perceptions, with a focus on climate policy misperception as our central case study. Although a majority of Americans support policies to mitigate climate change, public perception often underestimates this support. We will explore how such misperceptions can arise from the structure of social networks.

course.title: Senior Thesis in Music
course.description:
Students will register for senior thesis in spring of their senior year. Full music faculty approval of performance or composition concentration required by spring of sophomore year. Prerequisite: instructor permission.
For general music majors: written thesis, 50 pages minimum.
For performance concentration majors: Senior Recital (minimum 50 minutes of repertoire representing several style periods with comprehensive program notes).
For composition concentration majors: Senior Recital of original compositions and portfolio of composition manuscripts (minimum 30 minutes with comprehensive program notes).

course.title: Senior Thesis in Music
course.description:
Students will register for senior thesis in spring of their senior year. Full music faculty approval of performance or composition concentration required by spring of sophomore year. Prerequisite: instructor permission.
For general music majors: written thesis, 50 pages minimum.
For performance concentration majors: Senior Recital (minimum 50 minutes of repertoire representing several style periods with comprehensive program notes).
For composition concentration majors: Senior Recital of original compositions and portfolio of composition manuscripts (minimum 30 minutes with comprehensive program notes).

course.title: China-Latin America Relations in
course.description: Since the turn of the 21st century, China's presence in Latin America and the Caribbean has been widely examined by scholars and policymakers alike. As a relationship founded on economic and financial interests, the study of this cross-Pacific relationship has brought forth discussions about Chinaâ¬"s role in Latin Americaâ¬"s development and economic process and, more broadly speaking, in the Global South. Today, after more than two decades, how has this relationship evolved and what are the implications for Latin American countries? What kind of relationship do Latin American countries have with Chinaâ¬is it one that reinforces dependency patterns? Most importantly, what have been Latin Americaâ¬"s responses to Chinaâ¬"s influence and what is the impact of this relationship on the regionâ¬"s partnerships with other traditional partners, especially in the context of increased U.S.-China tensions?

course.title: Spanish Transition Almodovar
course.description: Pedro Almodovar is one of the most recognizable auteur directors in Europe today. This course studies Pedro Almodovar's development from his directorial debut to the present, from the "shock" value of the early films to the award-winning mastery of the later ones. Prerequisite: Spanish 101.

course.title: Cognitive Psychology
course.description: Cognitive Psychology provides insight into how the mind works.  The major topics include perception, attention, memory, learning, imagery, language, knowledge and categorization, and decision-making.  The course will give you the ability to 1) think about the human mind in terms of mental processes; and 2) understand how science can build models of these mental processes using simple behaviors in highly creative ways.  Prerequisites: Psychology 52 or instructor permission.

course.title: Peru at the crossroads
course.description: The course will explore Peru through its history, politics, and vibrant cultural traditions. Through literature, political essays, film, visual art,  and activist media, students examine how colonialism, race, inequality, political conflict, and social movements have shaped Peruvian society. The course highlights diverse voices and perspectives to explore struggles over identity, memory, justice, and competing visions of Peru's past and future. Course meets Letters and Race and Ethnic Studies general education requirements.

course.title: Art, Gender, and Feminisms
course.description: How have theories and lived experiences of gender and sexuality shaped the production and reception of art? This seminar centers questions of identity, community, activism, and intersectionality in art practice, theory, and history in the United States since the end of World War II, with close engagement with feminist and queer theory and its intersections with social justice. We will consider how artists negotiate gender roles and politics in their work, refracting current events around them. Course meets Fine arts and Gender and Women's Studies general education requirements.

course.title: Imagine Aristotle in Arabic
course.description: Imagination is fundamental to literary studies, but what is it? Aristotle offers one answer. In this advanced seminar, we will study the Aristotelian imagination comparatively, by focusing on how classical Islamic thinkers like Avicenna and al-Ghazali repurposed Aristotle for philosophical, social, and spiritual projects that celebrated wonder. Prerequisite: Three courses total from literature, philosophy, and/or religious studies. Texts in English. Greek/Arabic skills welcome. Course meets Letters general education requirement.

course.title: Enlightenment's Material Worlds
course.description: An introduction to the French Enlightenment through the lens of material culture. Our study of three material objects-chintz, sofas, and porcelain-will allow you to understand the French Enlightenment's connection to free and unfree labor, consumerism and global trade, while making connections with hyper consumption in our own times. Themes include Enlightenment notions of labor and leisure; European constructions of race; prestige, gender, sex, and performance. Conducted in French. Course meets Letters general education requirement.

course.title: Paris Plays Itself
course.description: Paris is among the most filmed and mythologized cities in cinematic history. Inspired by Thom Andersen's celebrated 2003 film, Los Angeles Plays Itself, which draws on scenes filmed in Los Angeles to reveal the city's hidden history, this course interweaves the history of French cinema with that of the City of Light to examine how filmmakers from different eras and communities have reinvented Paris, revealing the conflicts and contradictions that cinematic myths about the city so often obscure. Course meets Letter general education requirement.

course.title: Making It Work
course.description: Who makes the global economy work? This course examines women's labor at the intersection of gender, race, migration, and political economy. From nail salons and nursing homes to domestic work and street vending, we trace how gendered and racialized occupational niches were historically made-and why the global economy came to depend on them. We also ask how women have navigated, adapted to, and transformed these economies through networks, knowledge, and entrepreneurship. Course meets Social Science general education requirement.

course.title: La Commedia in Italia
course.description: This course will explore the tradition of Italian comedy from Dante, Boccaccio and the early modern theatre, to contemporary film and television. Through close readings, screenings, and discussions, students will examine how Italian comedians, playwrights, filmmakers, and performers used humor, satire and parody to reflect and challenge social, political, and cultural realities. Course meets Letters general education requirement.

course.title: Queer Code: Microbes 2 Microsoft
course.description: Advanced Topics: Queer Code: Microbes 2 Microsoft. This course historicizes the presumed divide between biology and technology. From Leibniz's logic to Boolean algebra, binary numbers to quettabytes, and automatons to AI , queer code is addressed in at least three ways: 1) as racialized, gendered, sexual, and embodied transgressions historically coded in public spaces, 2) as women, queer, and trans developers and computer end-users, and 3) as anti-racist feminist-queer-trans analyses of science, media, and technology studies. Prerequisite: FGSS/GWS 026 or 036 recommended. Course meets Gender and Women's Studies general education requirement.

course.title: Wittgenstein
course.description: This is an advanced seminar on one of the most influential thinkers of the 20th century, Ludwig Wittgenstein. We will focus on his later phase, primarily the Philosophical Investigations and On Certainty. Familiarity with analytic philosophy of language will be assumed. Topics include language, meaning, rule following, the mind, sensation, relativism, knowledge/certainty, doubt, the limits of philosophy, and worldviews. Prerequisites: Philosophy of Language, Logic are recommended. Course meets Letters general education requirement.

course.title: Qualitative Methods
course.description: This course is intended to be an overview of qualitative research designs and analyses in psychology. We will address the epistemological stance of qualitative methods in psychology, design considerations for diverse qualitative methods, and analytical steps within specific qualitative methods. In addition to understanding the prominent qualitative designs in psychology, we will also attend to the overall place of qualitative methods in psychology. Students must also register in PSYC146L SC. Course has prerequisites.

course.title: Risk and Resilience
course.description: This course will examine topics such as the risks posed to development by poverty, homelessness, parental mental health issues, domestic violence and abuse. We will also study ways to support resiliency in children in the face of these concerns. Students will be carrying out internships with related community agencies in Ontario that focus on children and families. Prerequisite: Psych 10

course.title: Qualitative Methods Lab
course.description: This lab course is required to be taken in conjunction with Psychology 146. The lab is designed to deepen you understanding of qualitative methods through pilot data collection and analysis. You will collect pilot data. You will, over the course of the semester, apply the skills learned in Psych 146 to analyze qualitative data in this lab. You will be tasked with developing a qualitative pilot study that adheres to a qualitative method overviewed in the class.

course.title: Christianity, Women, & Politics
course.description:
This course offers an intensive examination of the historical development of women's status and au-thority between the first and twenty-first centuries in a select few polities, including the Roman Em-pire, western European medieval and Reformation states, and the modern United States.
Tutorial courses meet every other week for about 60-90 minutes if a single-person tutorial/every week for two-person tutorials. Students will receive a set bibliographical resource list that will assist them. Course meets Gender and Women's Studies and Letters general education requirements.

course.title: Careers and Religious Studies
course.description: RLST 199C offers meetings and discussions every other week for seven sessions to assist students majoring/minoring in Religious Studies with navigating professional life and careers. The seminar includes opportunities to consider how a RLST degree can be used for professional success. This course particularly emphasizes practical components for navigating the job market, including crafting and/or revising a CV/Resume, how to write cover letters, mock job interviews, negotiation strategies, etc. Course may be taken twice for credit.

course.title: Metaphor and Analogy
course.description: We often associate metaphor and analogy with decoration in creative writing.  But we live by metaphors every day.  Scientists explain complex and unintuitive ideas through metaphor.  Politicians use metaphors to create the frameworks for their legislation and their election campaigns.  Attorneys and judges routinely appeal to a system of case law rooted in analogy.  In this course, we'll study how metaphor and analogy shape how we experience and think about the world.

course.title: Alone Together: Poetic Collab
course.description: Special Topic: Alone Together: Poetic Collab. Though writing may require solitude, writers are in conversation with the world and its writers. In this workshop, poets are researchers, and your influences, preoccupations, and forms guide our inventions and revisions, from writing footnotes or homages, with computer or classmate. Intensive reading, writing, and peer feedback is essential.

course.title: Underworlds and Otherworlds
course.description: Understood as "the art of the possible," politics represents the negotiation of competing interests and demands within a constrained system of electoral rules and governance procedures. In contrast, this course will explore forms of politics that contest the boundaries of the possible, unsettle shared understandings of the real, and engage in the prefigurative work of bringing future worlds into being. Underworlds: the fugitive space of evasion and escape. Otherworlds: the future taking shape. Course meets Social Science general education requirement.

course.title: The Age of Catastrophes
course.description: Do we live in an age of catastrophes? How can we apprehend a present marked by crises, disasters, and catastrophes? What does it mean to inhabit a world that might be ending? This course explores the politics of catastrophe, crisis, and disaster across space and time. Themes include environmental disasters, capitalism, technology, and colonialism. The course is organized in three movements: theorizing catastrophe, examining different events, and exploring resistance in catastrophic times. Course meets Social Science general education requirement.

course.title: Vietnamese Language and Culture
course.description:
This multilevel course approaches Vietnamese as a living social practice and welcomes students across proficiency levels, from those encountering Vietnamese for the first time to heritage speakers and students with intermediate or advanced proficiency. Students develop speaking, listening, reading, and writing through differentiated activities and assignments that build from their individual linguistic backgrounds while creating opportunities to learn with and from one another.
Language learning is situated within the study of Vietnamese cultures and communities. Through film, music, literature, visual and popular culture, everyday communication, and other authentic materials and encounters, students explore how language reflects and shapes social relationships, identities, histories, and contemporary life in Vietnam and Vietnamese communities. Classroom work emphasizes meaningful communication, collaboration, cultural inquiry, and engagement with different perspectives and experiences.
Students develop linguistic proficiency and intercultural understanding while learning to communicate across social and cultural contexts. Open to all students interested in Vietnamese language and culture, the course is especially relevant for students considering the Pitzer in Vietnam Summer Program, where they can continue their learning through sustained engagement with Vietnamese host families, communities, and local partners.

course.title: Queer Histories in the US
course.description: Focusing on the twentieth century U.S., this course explores the historical experiences of people we might today consider lesbian, bisexual, gay, trans, and queer (LGBTQ+). We will examine how these communitiesâ¬ and the identity categories that define themâ¬were shaped by complex economic, cultural, and legal factors. Topics include the medicalization of homosexuality and gender variance, urbanization, nightlife, labor, state persecution, queer migrations, liberation movements, HIV/AIDS, and the influence of race and class on sexual/gender identity and community formation. The course will provide critical historical context for contemporary societal anxieties about same-sex marriage, drag, and transition-related healthcare.

course.title: Environmental Demography
course.description: Why are many of the most climate-risky areas, like coastlines and deserts, also places with the fastest-growing populations? In this class, we will use quantitative methods to examine topics like population change, hazard exposure, risk management, and other demographic trends. Students will replicate existing research and contribute to data collection efforts.

course.title: Follow the Money
course.description: This course investigates money as a central object of social and political life. We follow the money through its different forms, from national currencies to digital monies, and trace how money moves across sites, from central banks to borders. Drawing from politics, anthropology, geography, and media studies, this course links texts, methodological exercises, and multimedia materials to examine how money ties everyday life to global processes today. Course meets Social Science GE.

course.title: 9/11: Histories and Afterlives
course.description: What happens when we treat 9/11 not only as an event, but as a historical archive? Moving backward and forward from September 11, 2001, this course explores its deeper histories-from U.S. empire and globalization to the lives and labor behind the Twin Towers-and its afterlives in war, immigration, surveillance, and memory. Throughout, we ask: How do we historicize a recent, contested past whose actors and consequences are still with us? Course meets Social Science and Race and Ethnic Studies general education requirements.

course.title: Narrating The Self
course.description: Our memories provide us with more than a record of the past. They help us construct a sense of self, explain how we came to become that person, and imagine who we might become. In this seminar, we will examine the relationship between memory, identity, and psychological disorder. We will consider how experiences become organized into representations of the self, while asking how remembering is also shaped by families, communities, and cultures. We will examine how these processes differ across forms of psychopathology, including depression, PTSD, and personality pathology. Throughout the course, we will treat memory and psychopathology as reciprocal: psychological symptoms shape what and how we remember, while the organization and retrieval of memories may themselves maintain patterns of thought, emotion, and behavior. We will return to a fundamental question: when memory changes, in what sense does the self change with it?

course.title: Natural Products
course.description: This course provides an introduction to reactions and strategies for the synthesis of complex molecules with an emphasis on natural products. It will bridge the gap between foundational organic chemistry and the real world, where syntheses rarely go according to plan. Students will learn to move beyond linear thinking by looking at a complex molecule and deconstructing it backwards. The course will draw from current literature and case studies significant to the historical development of the field to teach students how to troubleshoot synthetic roadblocks.

course.title: Toxicity, Secrecy, Agency
course.description: From covert insurgency agents to toxic chemical agents, this course considers "agents" from multiple angles to uncover the insidious consequences of empire and the forms of agency made possible in literature and art to expose, resist, and commemorate. Our study will be grounded in histories of colonization and decolonial resistance in the French-speaking world, but we will specifically focus on three cases of empire's ongoing environmental impact: nuclear tests in the Sahara and Pacific, pesticides in the Caribbean (chlordecone/Kepone), and herbicides in Southeast Asia (e.g., Agent Orange). How have writers, artists, activists, and everyday people responded to these less visible forms of colonial violence? How do those responses inherit a legacy of counter-violent insurgency? What do their narrative strategies, aesthetic innovations, and political mobilizations teach us about possibilities for global solidarity in the face of ecological collapse?

course.title: California Poets
course.description: A Survey of selected California poets of the 20th and 21st centuries.

course.title: Friedrich Nietzsche
course.description: This class will be an exploration of the thought, writings and times of the great German writer, scholar and philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche (1844-1900). We will look at Nietzsche's ideas on classical antiquity, Christian morality, evolution, drama, personality, madness, suffering, art, science, philosophy, psychology and the future.

course.title: Friedrich Nietzsche
course.description: This class will be an exploration of the thought, writings and times of the great German writer, scholar and philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche (1844-1900). We will look at Nietzsche's ideas on classical antiquity, Christian morality, evolution, drama, personality, madness, suffering, art, science, philosophy, psychology and the future.

course.title: Microbiology
course.description:
Despite being almost entirely invisible, microbes are the dominant form of life on earth. Microbes have terraformed our planet, caused devastating diseases, and likely created your favorite cheese. This course will act as an introduction to microbial evolution, cell biology, genetics, physiology, and metabolism. We will use these concepts to help explain the diversity, ecology, and impact of microbes in environments such as human infections, gut microbiomes, and agricultural soil. While this course will focus on bacteria, we will briefly discuss archaea, viruses, and eukaryotic microorganisms. This offering does not fulfill the seminar requirement for HMC Biology majors.

Prerequisite: BIOL113  HM or instructor permission. HMC students only, students from other Claremont Colleges require instructor permission.

course.title: Organismal Biology Lab
course.description:
This lab course will provide the framework for studying how organisms operate and interact with the world around them. We will cover topics including biodiversity, morphology, physiology, behavior, evolution, and ecology. After learning and practicing various lab and field techniques, students will complete a collaborative, multifaceted research project involving the organismal biology of animals at the Bernard Field Station. This offering fulfills a Biology lab course requirement for HMC Biology majors, but does not fulfill the seminar requirement.

Prerequisites: BIOL054  HM and BIOL154  HM
Corequisite: One of BIOL101  HM, BIOL108  HM, OR BIOL109  HM

course.title: Memory Disorders and Dementia
course.description: This seminar will examine memory disorders and dementia from a neuropsychological perspective. Topics will include amnesia, neuroanatomy of memory, evaluation of patients with memory loss, neuropsychology of Alzheimer's disease, and other dementia syndromes.

course.title: Physical Chem IIB: Material Chem
course.description: This course covers "macroscopic" physical chemistry topics, including materials chemistry, phase transitions, metastable materials, non-covalent interactions (particularly at surfaces and interfaces), the thermodynamic and kinetic behavior of bulk materials, and structure-property relationships. Prerequisite: CHEM051  HM.

course.title: Introduction to Computer Science
course.description: IIntroduction to the heart  of computer science. Students engage in computational problem-solving techniques and gain experience with the design, implementation, testing, and documentation of programs in a high-level language. In addition, students learn to design digital devices, program in a small machine language, recognize computing's inherent limitations, and understand how computers operate in practice. Societal and ethical issues related to computer science are central.

course.title: Agents, Software, Collaboration
course.description:
Agents, Software, Collaboration will give students practice collaborating with AI agents to develop and deliver capable software systems. Some of these systems will be individual projects. Others will be motivated by external stakeholders, involving further collaboration with those stakeholders and fellow students. Students will explore different interfaces and workflows for specifying, iterating, and taking accountability for the software systems they build. Alongside the projects, the course will develop an understanding of the underlying generative models (LLMs) and their scaffolding. A central course goal is that all students emerge with a portfolio that illustrates their comfort with and capacity to deploy agentic toolsets, knowledgeably and responsibly, on future professional projects.
Prerequisite: CSCI005  HM.

course.title: Programming Languages
course.description: A thorough examination of issues and features in language design and implementation, including how to represent a program as data, how to parse a program, how to implement scope, and how to interpret and compile a program. Additional topics will be selected from: historical and cultural aspects of programming languages; various implementation techniques such type checking, memory management, optimization, concurrency, or those specific to a programming paradigm (e.g., functional or object-oriented); additional topics related to programming languages at the discretion of the instructor. Prerequisite: Computer Science 70 and 81.

course.title: Germany Black and White
course.description: Drawing on literary texts, media debates, film and visual culture, historical sources, and everyday experiences, this cultural-studies and politics course examines contemporary discussions of race and racism in the German-speaking world. Situating questions of race, migration, xenophobia, and class within their specific German cultural and historical contexts, the course offers students new perspectives on familiar questions. Taught in German and English.

course.title: Making Computer Science
course.description: This course will explore historical and modern connections between computer science and making. Students will participate in readings, discussions, and lots of hands-on creating. We'll spend most of our time in the HMC Makerspace, learning how to use tools like 3D-printers, laser cutters, waterjet cutters, and the digital jacquard loom. We will learn about the file formats underlying each of these tools, and explore ways that computer science skills can be leveraged in making. We will also read papers connecting textile work to the history of computer science, and explore current research related to fabrication and computational crafting. A significant component of the course will be a project that uses one or more of the tools introduced in the course to create a new model, demonstration, or artwork related to a computer science concept. Prerequisite: CSCI070  HM.

course.title: Retrocomputing and Emulation
course.description: This course explores the foundations of modern computing through the lens of retrocomputing and emulation. Retrocomputing allows us to revisit the pioneering technologies of the past, from early mainframes and minicomputers to the iconic 8-bit microcomputers that revolutionized personal computing. Emulation allows us to recreate these systems in software, providing a hands-on experience with early computer environments that wouldn't otherwise be accessible. In this course, students will not only get hands-on experience working with (and writing code for) these vintage systems but will also gain a deep understanding of the principles that underpin modern computing. In particular, the 8-bit machines of the 1980s allow us to understand "the whole enchilada" of a computer system, from hardware to software, in a way that is difficult to achieve with modern systems. Students will also gain understanding and experience working with the software that emulates these systems, as well as the challenges and opportunities that come with it. The construction of "virtual machines" (in this case virtual retro machines) is an enduring topic in computer science with broad applications beyond retrocomputing. A final project will allow students to apply their knowledge, potentially creating demos, or exploring hardware emulation. As a new offering, student input will help shape the course's direction. Prerequisites: CSCI070  HM; CSCI105  HM is recommended.

course.title: Computing Education Research
course.description: An introduction to computing education research. Participants in this seminar-style course will read foundational literature in the field that explores what is known about how students learn within computer science. Equitable grading methods and their usage in computing courses is a particular focus of this class. The course will also provide an introduction to qualitative research methods: as part of a course project, students will carry out interviews and employ qualitative methods to analyze the resulting data. Prerequisites: Prerequisites: CSCI070  HM or CSCI062  PO and junior or senior standing.

course.title: Design,Computing,HumanExperience
course.description: This course examines computing as a form of design and human-computer interaction as a historical, philosophical, and cultural phenomenon. Rather than treating interfaces as neutral tools or HCI as a collection of design techniques, we will look at how computers have reshaped ideas about thought, action, communication, embodiment, work, and everyday life, as well as how those things have reshaped how we think of computing.

course.title: Intro Engr Design/Manufacturing
course.description: Design problems are, typically, open-ended and ill-structured. Students work in small teams applying techniques for solving design problems that are, normally, posed by not-for-profit clients. The project work is enhanced with lectures and reading on design theory and methods, and introduction to manufacturing techniques, project management techniques and engineering ethics. Enrollment limited to first-year students and sophomores, or by permission of the instructor. Prerequisite: Writing 1. Corequisite: Physics 24.

course.title: Intro Engr Design/Manufact Lab
course.description: Required lab to accompany ENGR004  HM.

course.title: Continuum Mechanics
course.description: The fundamentals of modeling continuous media, including: stress, strain and constitutive relations; elements of tensor analysis; basic applications of solid and fluid mechanics (including beam theory, torsion, statically indeterminate problems and Bernoulli's principle); application of conservation laws to control volumes. Prerequisite: Engineering 79 and Physics 24.

course.title: Elec & Magnetic Circuits/Devices
course.description: Introduction to the fundamental principles underlying electronic devices and applications of these devices in circuits. Topics include electrical properties of materials; physical electronics (with emphasis on semiconductors and semiconductor devices); passive linear electrical and magnetic circuits; active linear circuits (including elementary transistor amplifiers and the impact of non-ideal characteristics of operational amplifiers on circuit behavior); operating point linearization and load-line analysis; electromagnetic devices such as transformers. Prerequisite: Engineering 79.

course.title: Heat & Mass Transfer
course.description: Integrated approach to heat and mass transfer through the study of the governing equations common to both fields. Principles of conduction, diffusion, convection, and radiation and their use in engineering design and analysis. An overview of chemical separation process design. Applications drawn from a wide variety of engineering disciplines, including environmental, biomedical, mechanical, and chemical engineering. Prerequisite: ENGR082  HM.

course.title: Operations Research
course.description: Linear, integer, non-linear and dynamic programming, classical optimization problems, and network theory. Prerequisites: Mathematics 73. (Crosslisted as MATH187  HM)

course.title: Stochastic Modeling: Indust Sys
course.description: Modeling approaches for analyzing the behavior and performance of systems characterized by uncertainty. Major topics include Poisson arrival processes, discrete and continuous time Markov chains, Queueing systems, and System Reliability estimation, with applications to production systems design and manufacturing performance. Prerequisites: MATH056  HM or MATH062  HM or equivalent.

course.title: Energy & the Environment
course.description:
This course is an introduction to quantitative concepts related to energy and the environment. It covers current and future demands for energy; methods of power generation including fossil fuels, nuclear, and renewables; associated detrimental by-products; and advanced strategies to improve power densities, efficiencies, and emissions. The course covers the critical issues facing energy extraction, cultivation, transformation, transportation, consumption, disposal, environmental impacts, and policy. 

Prerequisite: ENGR082  HM

course.title: DigComm Using SoftwareDefRadios
course.description:
An applied introduction to digital communication systems using software-defined radio (SDR) technology with GNU Radio and hardware transceivers. The primary objective of this course is to cover the full end-to-end transmitter and receiver pipeline so that students can capture, synchronize, and decode real-world over-the-air digital communication signals by the end of the semester. Course topics include source encoding, channel encoding, digital modulation and symbol mapping, pulse shaping, complex baseband (I/Q) representation, and system imperfection handling techniques, such as carrier offset recovery and stochastic channel modeling. 

Prerequisites: ENGR072  HM, ENGR079  HM, AND ENGR101  HM

course.title: Problem Solving with AI
course.description:
Professional skills for solving engineering problems with AI. Topics include data analysis, website development, team-based software development with coding agents and shared repositories, and agentic design automation. Hands-on projects intended for students with little previous AI experience. HP/P/NP grading only. 

Prerequisite(s): Junior or Senior Standing

course.title: Bio Signal Processing
course.description:
This course applies systems theory and signal processing to real physiological signals that students record themselves. Students learn how raw measurements of the heart, muscles, and body become reliable, interpretable health information. Hands-on assignments put each technique into practice right away on students own data, including work with mobile apps (no prior knowledge of app design is expected). In the final project, students use AI tools deliberately and critically to build and validate a complete biosignal analysis pipeline. Specific topics may include: filtering and denoising, statistical foundations for biosignal analysis, bias and equity in health sensing, feature engineering and selection, introductory machine learning, including multivariate regression, classification, clustering, and principal component analysis

Prerequisite: ENGR101 HM

course.title: Intro to Aircraft Design
course.description:
Introduction to Aircraft Design provides terminology, principles, and logic to engage in design trades upon entering the aerospace industry. Sizing and flight dynamics are followed by aircraft systems  propulsion, fuel, flight controls, landing gear, power distribution, structures, avionics, etc  then those are wrapped into human factors, safety, manufacturing, and operations considerations. A single aircraft type will be quantitatively examined throughout to clearly envision trades and the certification process.

Prerequisite: ENGR083  HM

course.title: Advanced Structural Dynamics
course.description: Free and forced response of continuous systems, including the vibration of strings, rods, shafts, membranes, beams and plates. One dimensional finite element methods: discretization of a continuum, selection of interpolation functions, and determining the element mass and stiffness matrices and the corresponding load vector. Introduction to special topics, including the effects of parameter uncertainties on the dynamics of periodic structures and model updating in structural dynamics. Prerequisite: Engineering 171.

course.title: Anthropology of Futures
course.description: Do you imagine a future run over by AI and robots, climate catastrophe, and political apocalypse? Or is it a future that is kinder and more peaceful? From dystopias to utopias, imaginations of futures have held an important role in scientific and technological developments, education, policymaking, and social movements. This course uses the lens of ethnography to examine how  futures are engaged with in science and technology, public health, medicine, design, divination, policy, and grassroots social movements. Focusing on visions of anti-colonial, anti-racist, indigenous, postcolonial, and feminist futures, this seminar asks who gets to envision a future, and who gets to implement it?

course.title: Projects
course.description: This student driven art class consists of proposing, developing and presenting individual art projects. Medium specific and/or conceptually oriented projects are welcome. In addition to producing art, students will engage in research and written statements in regards to the ideas and related histories of their projects. Instructor permission is required to register. Please indicate previous art experience, a description of your project, and a link to examples of art you have created in your permission request.

course.title: Intro Asian Amer Hist:1850-Pres
course.description:
This survey course examines the history of Asian immigrant groups and their American-born descendants as they have settled and adjusted to life in the United States since 1850.  We will explore issues such as the experience of immigration, daily life in urban ethnic enclaves, and racist campaigns against Asian immigrants.  In addition, this course utilizes an ethnic studies framework that requires students to critically explore other themes such as class, community, empire, gender, labor, race, sexuality, settler colonialism, and war from the perspective of Asian Americans.

HSA Writing Intensive: No

course.title: Principles of Macroeconomics
course.description:
An introductory course designed to provide a fundamental understanding of the national economy. Topics include theories of unemployment, growth, inflation, income distribution, consumption, savings, investment, and finance markets, and the historical evolution of economic institutions and macroeconomic ideas.

HSA Writing Intensive: No

course.title: Translation/Foreignness of Lang
course.description:
This seminar is designed to introduce students to the foreignness of language through literary translation theory and its praxis. Participants will develop individual projects that will be revised and workshopped over the course of the semester. Weekly readings, including essays by theoreticians, accomplished writer-translators, and selections of multiple translations of a single text, will be used to familiarize students with a range of perspectives on translation and its relationship to writing. Prerequisite: Students must have reading knowledge of at least one foreign language.

HSA Writing Intensive: Yes

course.title: Third Cinema
course.description:
Emerging in Latin America in the 1960s and 1970s, the notion of Third Cinema takes its inspiration from the Cuban revolution and from Brazil's Cinema Novo. Third Cinema is the art of political film making and represents an alternative cinematic practice to that offered by mainstream film industries. This course explores the aesthetics of film making from a revolutionary consciousness in three regions: Africa, Asia, and Latin America. 

HSA Writing Intensive: No

course.title: KnowledgeUnderstanding&CogSucces
course.description: This course explores what it is to know something, to understand it, and to believe it rationally, and why these forms of cognitive success are valuable. We will examine competing accounts of these achievements and the means by which they are attained, including theories of justification, evidence, and intellectual virtue. Topics may include skepticism, the structure of knowledge, the role of testimony (especially in scientific contexts), and probabilistic models of rational belief.

course.title: Climate Crisis&Disaster Politics
course.description: An examination of how political systems in the United States influence and are influenced by climate disasters. In this course, we will explore who is in charge of disaster response and preparedness, how definitions of nature and of disasters shape the policy process, and who is impacted most during and after a disaster. We will ask how risk perceptions and experiences with climate disasters influence political attitudes and behaviors, tracing the electoral consequences of recent heat waves, floods, fires, and hurricanes.

course.title: Sociology of Friendship
course.description: What is friendship and how is it socially produced? Why does society value romantic relationships more than platonic friendships? How can sociology help us understand thorny, complicated aspects of friendship like money, envy, and group dynamics? In this course, we will explore these questions and more, looking at friendship in relation to: gender, race, age, class, ethnicity, sexual identity, (dis)ability, capitalism, imperialism, AI, globalization, climate change, etc.

course.title: Public Speaking/Sci & Citizenshp
course.description:
This course builds student speaking skills in three areas: communicating advanced topics in science and technology to non-specialists; speaking out on questions of politics and values; and engaging the intersection of the two through presentations on technically intensive social controversies. 

HSA Writing Intensive: No

course.title: Walking for Wellness
course.description: See the CMS Athletics web site for course description.

course.title: Math Methods in Data Science
course.description:
In this course, students will learn about common mathematical representations of data, the mathematical foundations of matrix factorization and tensor decomposition, and their application to many tasks in machine learning and data science. These decomposition techniques are integral tools in studying large-scale and multi-modal data and form the basis for many approaches to the topic modeling, dimension reduction, and clustering tasks. Potential topics include PCA, nonnegative matrix factorization, higher-order SVD, nonnegative tensor decompositions, K-means clustering, optimization techniques for these models, and applications in machine learning, data science, signal processing, and network science. 
Prerequisites: MATH019 HM (or equivalent course in multivariable calculus) and MATH073 HM (or equivalent course in linear algebra). MATH151  HM is recommended but not required.

course.title: Dem. Transitions Middle East
course.description: This course analyzes dynamics of authoritarianism and democratization in the Middle East and beyond. The course will be divided into three sections: the first covers the main theoretical perspectives explaining the persistence of authoritarian rule in the Middle East and other regions of the world (i.e. the cultural approach centered on value systems and religion; the structural approach centered on oil and other natural resources; and the institutional approach centered on civil-military relations and coercive agencies). The second section will ponder the theory and practice of non-violent challenges to authoritarian regimes. And the third section will study processes of authoritarian breakdown and consolidation during the 2011 Arab uprisings and their aftermath. Prerequisite: GOVT020 CM or instructor permission.

course.title: Afro-Pessimism Politics of Hope
course.description: This course will survey the deep and dark history of dreams, accomplishments and roadblocks that have constituted and continue to influence the ways Blacks in America negotiate a compromised political position. Traversing history from the brutality of the captured slave, to reformation and Jim Crow, to the Civil Rights movement and the modern day reflections on the role of civil society, police, and entertainment; we will reflect on the desires, goals, and hurdles that Blacks have faced all the while trying to articulate a sense of freedom within a white supremacist regime by following two lines of political thought: a Politics of Hope and Afro-Pessimism.

course.title: Foundations of Elec and Mag
course.description: An introduction to the physical principles governing electric and magnetic phenomena. Describing how charged particles in static and dynamic equilibria give rise to fields, potentials and forces, including applications of circuits and motors. Unification of Maxwell's equations, wave properties of light and further topics and time permits.

course.title: Graph Theory
course.description: An introduction to graph theory with applications. Theory and applications of trees, matchings, graph coloring, planarity, graph algorithms, and other topics. Prerequisites: Mathematics 73 and Mathematics 55.

course.title: Africana Philosophy
course.description: Philosophical thought and the philosophical cannon cannot be restricted to the 'great thinkers' of western history. This course will be a general introduction to Africana Philosophy. We will unveil not only that philosophy is more than the western world and has points of origin in other places, such as Africa, but we will also discover how Africana philosophy serves as a challenge to the integrity of integral concepts and themes in modern western philosophy; for example, the subject, freedom, the human, and even ontology. We will achieve these insights through a survey of thinkers, writers, and people who address themes such as traditional africana thought, black existentialism, black feminism, post colonialism, whiteness, double consciousness, and afro-pessimism. Cross-listed as PHIL109 CM.

course.title: Chin Gam Cul & Digit Trans
course.description: This course is designed to help students further develop their Chinese language skills while exploring the growing cultural, technological, and social significance of gaming among Chinese-speaking communities around the world. The course introduces students to an important area of contemporary Chinese language and culture that crosses geographic, national, and cultural boundaries. More specifically, it focuses on the social and cultural changes shaped by gaming culture and the critical role of technology in driving these changes, reshaping Chinese-speaking communities, and strengthening their connections with the wider world.

course.title: Cmplx Variables/Integral Trnsfrm
course.description: Complex differentiation, Cauchy-Riemann equations, Cauchy integral formulas, residue theory, Taylor and Laurent expansions, conformal mapping, Fourier and Laplace transforms, inversion formulas, other integral transforms, applications to solutions of partial differential equations. Prerequisites: Mathematics 73 and Mathematics 82.

course.title: Probability
course.description: Probability spaces, discrete and continuous random variables, conditional and marginal distributions, independence, expectation, generating functions, transformations, central limit theorem. Prerequisite: (MATH019  HM or equivalent) and (MATH073  HM (or equivalent) or permission of the instructor).

course.title: Undergraduate Mathematics Forum
course.description:
The goal of this course is to improve students' ability to communicate mathematics, both to a general and technical audience. Students will present material on assigned topics and have their presentations evaluated by students and faculty. This
format simultaneously exposes students to a broad range of topics from modern and classical mathematics.

course.title: Statistical Inference
course.description:
An introduction to the theory of statistical inference. Point estimation: Sufficiency, optimal unbiased estimation, method of moments, maximum likelihood. Interval estimation and hypothesis testing: Neyman-Pearson paradigm, most powerful and uniformly most powerful tests, (generalized) likelihood ratio tests, Wald and score tests, multiple testing, pivotal quantities and CDF inversion, the bootstrap. Applications to regression modeling. Bayesian perspectives and frequentist asymptotic theory will be presented throughout the course.

Prerequisites: MATH151 HM or MATH157 HM.

course.title: Time Series
course.description: An introduction to the theory of statistical time series. Topics include decomposition of time series, seasonal models, forecasting models including causal models, trend models, and smoothing models, autoregressive (AR), moving average (MA), and integrated (ARIMA) forecasting models. Time permitting we will also discuss state space models, which include Markov processes and hidden Markov processes, and derive the famous Kalman filter, which is a recursive algorithm to compute predictions. Statistical software will be used as a tool to aid calculations required for many of the techniques. Prerequisites: Permission of instructor.

course.title: Commutative Algebra
course.description: Topics include Noetherian rings, primary decomposition, localization, module theory, exact sequences, tensor products, homology, Ext, Tor, and key results like the Krull Altitude Theorem and the Snake Lemma. Additional topics may include depth, Krull dimension, Cohen-Macaulay rings, Gorenstein rings, complete intersection rings, and regular rings. Prerequisite: MATH171  HM or equivalent.

course.title: Senior Thesis in Mathematics
course.description: Senior thesis offers the student, guided by the faculty advisor, a chance to experience a taste of the life of a professional research mathematician. The work is largely independent with guidance from the research advisor. The principal objective of the senior thesis program is to help you develop intellectually and improve your written and verbal communication skills.  Students are expected to present their work orally and to produce a thesis conforming to the publication standards of a professional mathematician. Prerequisite(s): Senior standing as a mathematics major and permission from the Mathematics Senior Thesis Coordinator.

course.title: Polyhedral Combinatorics
course.description:
How can geometry help us count, organize, and optimize? This course explores the interplay between discrete mathematics and geometry through polytopes, the higher-dimensional relatives of polygons. We will turn subsets, permutations, and graph matchings into geometric objects, then study what their faces, volumes, and integer points reveal about the combinatorics. Topics include convexity, duality, triangulations, and Ehrhart theory, which studies how the number of integer points in a polytope changes as it expands. Through visual examples, proofs, computer experiments, and a final exposition/research project, students will encounter open problems and connections to current research.

Prerequisites: MATH055  HM, MATH073  HM, and one additional proof-based math course (e.g., MATH131  HM or MATH171  HM). If you have taken only MATH055  HM or MATH073  HM and would like to take the course, please reach out to the instructor.

course.title: Algebraic Topology
course.description:
Algebraic Topology helps us to determine when two objects are topologically the same (i.e., can you continuously change one object to the other and vice versa). For instance, is the universe topologically a 3-dimensional sphere, or is it connected to itself in a different way?  We use algebra to help ushence the term algebraic topology. This course is an introduction to simplicial and singular homology theories, and a major theme is the connection between combinatorial and topological concepts. Topics include simplicial complexes, homology groups, exact sequences, chain maps, diagram chasing, Mayer-Vietoris sequences, Eilenberg-Steenrod axioms, Jordan curve theorem, and additional topics as time permits.

Prerequisites: Math 131. Corequisite: MATH171  HM (or permission of the instructor). MATH147  HM is recommended, but not required.

course.title: Numerical Differential Equations
course.description:
An introduction to the analysis, computer implementation, and applications of fundamental numerical techniques for both ordinary and partial differential equations. Topics include convergence, conditioning, stability, and measures of error; interpolation, numerical differentiation and integration; initial- and boundary-value problems for ordinary differential equations; linear multistep methods and Runge-Kutta methods for initial-value problems and their stability and convergence; elliptic, hyperbolic, and parabolic partial differential equations and some canonical numerical methods for each type. Additional topics may include spectral, finite volume, and finite elements methods, and applications such as fluid dynamics, quantitative finance, image processing, and heat or mass transfer.

This course will satisfy (1) the computational mathematics requirement for the Mathematics major at HMC, and (2) the scientific computation requirement for the Joint Math-Physics major at HMC.

Prerequisites: CSCI005  HM and MATH082  HM.

course.title: Design & Analysis of Experiments
course.description:
When analyzed appropriately, correlation in a properly designed randomized experiment DOES imply causation. This course provides a mathematical introduction to the modern theory of the design and analysis of experiments. Topics include: Potential outcomes, Neymanian and Fisherian inference, stratification, regression adjustment, rerandomization, Latin squares, factorial designs, and fractional factorial designs. Time permitting, modern concepts such as computer experiments, sequential experimentation (e.g., bandits), and quasi-experimental designs will also be covered. While the emphasis of the course is on fundamental mathematical understanding, connections will be made to applications in engineering, technology, medicine, social science, and beyond. Students in this course will also have the opportunity to design and analyze their own experiment to rigorously study a meaningful question in their own lives.

Prerequisites: MATH062  HM (or 4 or better on the AP statistics exam) or MATH151  HM or MATH157  HM, or permission of instructor. Some exposure to probability and using statistical software for computation will be helpful.

course.title: Physics Laboratory
course.description: This course emphasizes the evidence-based approach to understanding the physical world through hands-on experience, experimental design, and data analysis. Experiments are drawn from a broad range of physics subjects, with applications relevant to modern society and technology. Prerequisite: Physics 24.

course.title: Fields & Waves
course.description: The theory of deformable media. Field equations for elastic and fluid media and for conducting fluids in electromagnetic fields. Particular emphasis on body and surface wave solutions of the field equations. Prerequisite: Mathematics 180 or Physics 64.

course.title: Particle Physics
course.description: A survey of the forces, particles, and structure of the Standard Model of particle physics. Topics of study include: Feynman diagrams, rates of particle interactions, and particle physics experiments; relativistic quantum mechanics of particles with spin; massive particles and the Higgs mechanism; phenomena of the strong and weak interactions. Prerequisite: Physics 116.

course.title: Biophysics
course.description: Selected topics in biophysics focusing on active research in the field. Possible topics include: biolocomotion, membrane biophysics, imaging techniques. Seminar format. Prerequisite: Biology 46 and Physics 51. (Crosslisted as BIOL174 HM)

course.title: Varieties of Tragedy
course.description: The tragedies performed in the English public theaters of the Renaissance include some of the most beautiful, profound poetry ever written. In attempting to recreate classical tragedy, English poets created something quite different: they experimented with controversial ideas about the human condition, they depicted scenes of ordinary life along with stories of kings and heroes, they expanded the available range of stylistic registers, and they mixed comic effects with tragic ones. In this course, we will study plays by Marlowe, Shakespeare, Webster, and Middleton.

course.title: Senior Thesis in Physics
course.description: Original experimental or theoretical investigations in physics undertaken in consultation with a faculty member. Projects may be initiated by the student or by a faculty member. Present faculty research areas include astrophysics, biophysics, optics, solid-state and low-temperature physics, general relativity, quantum mechanics, particle physics, geophysics, and soft matter physics. Students are responsible for an oral presentation on progress and plans in the first half of the thesis research.

course.title: Senior Thesis in Physics
course.description: Original experimental or theoretical investigations in physics undertaken in consultation with a faculty member. Projects may be initiated by the student or by a faculty member. Present faculty research areas include astrophysics, biophysics, optics, solid-state and low-temperature physics, general relativity, quantum mechanics, particle physics, geophysics, and soft matter physics. Students are responsible for an oral presentation on progress and plans in the first half of the thesis research.

course.title: Senior Thesis in Physics
course.description: Original experimental or theoretical investigations in physics undertaken in consultation with a faculty member. Projects may be initiated by the student or by a faculty member. Present faculty research areas include astrophysics, biophysics, optics, solid-state and low-temperature physics, general relativity, quantum mechanics, particle physics, geophysics, and soft matter physics. Students are responsible for an oral presentation on progress and plans in the first half of the thesis research.

course.title: Climate for Global Citizenship
course.description:
Are you interested in the climate? Maybe a little uncertain about the global implications of climate change?  Do you sometimes wonder what you might do to contribute to interventions (and solutions?) that address the changes wrought by a warming planet?  Not sure where to start?  If you answer yes to some of these questions, then this course is for you because future leaderslike youare going to be looked to for guidance, inspiration, and answers in the coming years.
