In this course well survey some of the big ideas of climate science, look to the future of climate change, and discuss ways that we can create a more livable planet.

Freshman and Sophomores only. HP/P/NP grading.

course.title: Games for ClimateChange Literacy
course.description: Students will learn  to use human-computer interaction methodologies, behavioral theories, and the transformational framework to design climate change literacy games with the intention of inspiring positive behaviorial change in players. Each game will be grounded in climate change literature for the rationale and arguments students make about different game design decisions. An example of a transformational game is Wingspan, for which there is anecdotal evidence of players becoming bird and nature enthusiasts because of the game?s influence. Prerequisite: CSCI060 HM or CSCI054 PO or instructor permission. The course may build on CORE099  HM, CSCI120  HM, or coursework in environmental analysis, but does not require it. There will be no coding in this class. Juniors and seniors only.

course.title: Core Skills Workshop
course.description: Foundational quantitative skills are reinforced to prepare students for the HMC Core. Initial topics cover linear systems, logarithmic properties, and algebraic manipulation. Geometry and spatial reasoning are treated through similar triangles, right-triangle trigonometry, and vector decomposition on rotated axes. Differential and integral calculus concepts are reviewed, including rules for derivatives and integration techniques. These skills are then combined to solve multi-step problems from various STEM fields.

Geometry and spatial reasoning are treated through similar triangles, right-triangle trigonometry, and vector decomposition on rotated axes. Differential and integral calculus concepts are reviewed, including rules for derivatives and integration techniques. These skills are then combined to solve multi-step problems from various STEM fields.

course.title: Core Skills Workshop
course.description: Foundational quantitative skills are reinforced to prepare students for the HMC Core. Initial topics cover linear systems, logarithmic properties, and algebraic manipulation. Geometry and spatial reasoning are treated through similar triangles, right-triangle trigonometry, and vector decomposition on rotated axes. Differential and integral calculus concepts are reviewed, including rules for derivatives and integration techniques. These skills are then combined to solve multi-step problems from various STEM fields.

course.title: Media and Counter Culture
course.description: A counter culture is an oppositional movement grounded in mass politics and culture but to what end today? Here we will focus on two historic periods and movements, the 1930s in Weimar Germany and the 1968 uprisings in France and the US. We will examine Weimar media examples including the films of Lang and Brecht?s Three Penny Opera.  For 1968 we will consider the Situationists and Godard?s films, and then the SDS and hippies in the USA.  Finally, we will consider cultural opposition in our global digital media culture.

course.title: Video Games in Memory
course.description: The organizing question of this course is: How do we remember video games and how do we remember in video games? This course pursues answers to this central question by looking at the historical development of video gaming hardware and the development of memory as both a narrative concern and a ludic/ haptic mechanic, starting with Amnesia (1986), Cystalis (1990), and Final Fantasy VI (1994). When taken seriously as a narrative device, memory causes formal experimentation. The course will show students how memory developed as a major source of gameplay and narrative innovation. This course will explore Media Studies concepts such as: repetition, gaze, narrative theory, ludonarrative dissonance, analepsis, affect theory, trauma studies, and temporality. This course will ask students to play games in class and outside of class during prescribed lab times. How games teach us to remember and what they teach us to recall and confront is, ultimately, this course?s aims of inquiry.

course.title: Special Topics in Literature
course.description:
The topic for Spring 2027 is "Chronicling Co-Education at CMC: Our School Stories":

Before the CMC went coed in 1976, Dr. Mabel Benson, a scholar of Literature, wrote our first catalogue. Before CMC?s founding, women graduated from and taught at Pomona and Scripps. In ?Our School Stories,? you will undertake archival research to reveal how students, faculty, staff, and alumni made the Men?s College into Claremont McKenna. How did this change impact communities across the Cs? To pursue this question, we?ll dive into college records at Special Collections, survey a literary tradition that envisioned women?s education, and build towards publication and public speaking opportunities in collaboration with CMC?s 50th Anniversary Celebration of Co-Education.

course.title: Processes of Env Policymaking
course.description: This course focuses on how environmental, conservation, and natural-resource policies are developed and chosen in the policy processes of the United States and other countries.  This focus permits examination of the methodologies of evaluating environmental policy options, the processes of policymaking, and the institutions involved in conservation, environmental improvement, and other policies that affect the environment.  The analytic approaches include the policy sciences framework for understanding the process itself, the methodologies of ecosystem valuation, and the issues involved with different types of policy instruments for environmental and conservation management.  This course is cross-listed as Econ 118.

course.title: Processes of Env Policymaking
course.description: This course focuses on how environmental, conservation, and natural-resource policies are developed and chosen in the policy processes of the United States and other countries.  This focus permits examination of the methodologies of evaluating environmental policy options, the processes of policymaking, and the institutions involved in conservation, environmental improvement, and other policies that affect the environment.  The analytic approaches include the policy sciences framework for understanding the process itself, the methodologies of ecosystem valuation, and the issues involved with different types of policy instruments for environmental and conservation management.  This course is cross-listed as GOVT118.

course.title: Policymaking in Internatnl Orgs
course.description: This course examines the nature, processes, and implications of official international organizations and their growing role in international affairs.  How and why does multilateralism arise, what are the relationships between official international organizations and the member countries, how do they make decisions, what implications do these processes have on international cooperation and conflict?  The course will focus largely on international economic organizations such as the International Monetary Fund, the World Bank, and the World Trade Organization, but will also focus on mutual security and environmental organizations.

course.title: Senior Thesis in Psychology
course.description:
Selected seniors will be invited to conduct
research and to prepare a thesis.

course.title: Cognitive Psychology
course.description: An introduction to the psychological investigation of perceptual and cognitive processes, emphasizing pattern recognition, attention, memory, knowledge representation, problem solving, decision making, language, and intelligence. The goal of the course is to understand the processes by which humans acquire and maintain knowledge.

course.title: Introduction to Video Art
course.description: This class is an introduction to the fundamentals of video production, encouraging a creative approach to the medium through an open-ended engagement with different techniques and modalities found in documentary and other filmmaking practices. The goal is to familiarize students with the use of the video camera, microphones and sound recording equipment, tripod,and non-linear editing systems. The class is critique-driven: the discussions that follow the screening of each exercise are the principal method by which the successes and shortcomings of that work are evaluated. Students will create 5 2-minute video works. All assignments will be carefully explained long before the due date. Course meets Fine Arts general education requirement.

course.title: Laboratory, Inorganic Chemistry
course.description: Laboratory, Inorganic Chemistry

course.title: Adv Leadership & Management IA
course.description: This course develops student proficiency in planning, executing, and assessing complex operations, functioning as a member of a staff, and providing performance feedback to subordinates. Students assess risk, make ethical decisions, and lead fellow students. Lessons on military justice and personnel processes prepare students to make the transition to Army officers. Students analyze, evaluate, and instruct students in other Military Science and Leadership courses. Both their classroom and battalion leadership experiences are designed to prepare students for their first unit of assignment. Leadership lab and MSL 099  CM are required for all cadets.

course.title: High Energy Astrophysics
course.description: A survey of the physical processes and astrophysical systems that produce high-energy photons and presents a survey of the new ultraviolet, x-ray and gamma-ray observations. Topics include active galactic nuclei, black holes, neutron stars, supernova remnants and cosmic rays. Prerequisites: Astronomy 62 and Physics 52. Offered jointly with Pomona and Joint Sciences.

course.title: Latin American Politics & Policy
course.description: This course approaches the understanding of Latin America through the lens of how governments, other state institutions, and civil society organizations address the most prominent public policy challenges across the diverse Latin American contexts. These challenges range from basic governance issues such as democratization and civil-military relations, to socio-economic issues such as economic growth, social safety nets, and rights. In addition to readings and discussions about Latin America as a whole, particular attention will focus on Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Mexico, and Venezuela. Prerequisities: GOVT 060 CM.

course.title: Special Topics: Photography
course.description:
Alternative Processes | Eco-Photography
In this course we will explore the limits of photographic materiality through experimentation with natural plant-based emulsions, sun exposure, contact printin,, recycled materials, and organic paper making. In order to imagine a "no-waste" photographic future, we will look to the early history of photography, eco-poetics, and eco-feminist theories. Students will be engaged in collaborative studio projects as well as research, reading/discussion, group presentations, and a final group exhibition.

course.title: Introduction to B&W Photography
course.description: This is a comprehensive introduction to the practice of analog black and white photography with an emphasis on image production using a 35mm camera, B&W film, and wet darkroom processes. Students will be introduced to a broad range of historical and contemporary art photographers and consider how their own work might fit into this trajectory. A final self-directed research based project allows students to explore their own interests while developing a professional photographic portfolio.

course.title: Foundations of Data Sci with AI
course.description: This course will focus on importing, cleaning, and visualizing data. Students will learn how to sort, filter, and join datasets, as well as how to use a dataset to answer questions. We will use both traditional methods through SQL, Python/Pandas, and R, as well as AI tools.

course.title: Transportation Tech & Clim Polic
course.description:
High-quality transportation services are essential for our way of life. However, transportation is a major expense, causes significant negative side effects, and is now the largest source of greenhouse gas emissions in the United States. This course examines the complex system-of-systems that is modern transportation as well as the many technologies and policies that can mitigate the negative effects of transportation while maintaining or improving transportation services. These include cleaner and electric vehicles, lower emission fuels, and changes to travel demand. It also explores transportation's messy history of inequity and options to improve environmental justice. This course has a U.S. focus with a balance of technology and policy content and a strong interactive component.

Prerequisites: One course in chemistry (CHEM042 HM or CHEM014L KS or CHEM034L KS or CHEM001A PO) and one course in computer science (CSCI005 HM or CSCI004 PZ or CSCI051P PO or CSCI040 CM or DS 001 SC) and one course in calculus (MATH019 HM or MATH030 CM/PO/PZ/SC) and one course in mechanics (PHYS024 HM or PHYS030L KS or PHYS033L KS or PHYS071 PO or PHYS125 PO) and one course addressing thermodynamics (CHEM051 HM or ENGR082 HM or PHYS117 HM). Prerequisites can be waived by the instructor.

course.title: Interdisciplinary Special Topics
course.description:
Topic changes each semester.  The topic for Spring 2027 will be: "Gender and Sports"

An examination of the relationship of gender and sport through an interdisciplinary lens. Students will analyze how sport shapes and is shaped by societal understandings of gender and apply a gender/feminist analysis to key areas related to sport, including: biology and performance, media representation of gender in sports, equity and competition, gender inclusion, and the experiences of LGBTQ+ individuals.  Special attention will be paid to the influence of gender, race, class, and disability on sports.

course.title: Fascism: Politics and Histories
course.description: What is fascism? What are its origins? What are its practices? How do we know it when we see it?  What have been the political and social responses to it?  To explore these questions, this seminar considers the emergence, florescence, and limits  of fascism in 20th century Europe, particularly in Italy, Spain, and Germany. In doing so, it also considers fascismâ¬"s reception in the United States.

course.title: Environ/Health/SouthernAfrica
course.description:
"The central question of this course is: How have Southern African peoples made sense of their environments and their health, and how and why have these meanings changed across generations?  In particular, this course explores Southern African ecological and health philosophies, as well as changes brought about through intercultural contact, colonization, the expansion of capitalism, urbanization, Christian religious syncretism, the HIV/AIDS pandemic, and climate change.  We will especially focus on how such changes have impacted communities and family life in rural areas, paying close attention to new forms of social inequality and to the challenges of social reproduction across generations. Students will study works based in ethnographic and oral historical fieldwork, linking the experiences of individuals and communities to larger processes of social and environmental change.

Pitzer College first-years, sophomores, and juniors in the course will have the option to apply to participate in an in-country, community-engaged research project in Botswana during Summer 2027."

course.title: Sustainable Place Studio
course.description: This studio course will engage students in the integrative practices of design and planning toward the creation of a sustainable and resilient place. Critical analyses will be pair with projective approaches to (re)shape and adapt space in a built and planted project in redefined ecological, cultural, policy and technological settings.

course.title: Intro to Cognitive Science
course.description:
Cognitive science is the interdisciplinary study of the mind, traditionally drawing upon anthropology, biology, computer science, linguistics, philosophy, and psychology. In this introductory course, we survey historical and contemporary
debates concerning the nature of perception, language, and consciousness, among other topics, at the intersection of these disciplines.

course.title: Ideology & Political Ideologies
course.description: This course surveys major political ideologies (including liberalism, conservatism, socialism, etc). Before turning to these ideologies, the course examines competing conceptions of "ideology" itself, from Marx's concept of false consciousness, to Mannheim's view of ideology as a sociology of knowledge, to Geertz's view of ideology as a cultural system.

course.title: Economic Democracy
course.description: A  survey of foundational texts in economic democracy, a field concerned with extending democratic principles into economic life through mechanisms like worker cooperatives, workplace democracy, and participatory economic planning. The course draws on participatory democratic theory, institutional theory, and foundational texts in capitalism and socialism.

course.title: Topics in Aristotelianism
course.description: Aristotle held, contra Plato, that the good for us is a human good, that is, a good shaped by human nature. In this seminar, we will first carefully examine the various appeals to nature in Aristotle?s ethical writings, along with their metaphysical and psychological underpinnings. We will then turn to the early history of naturalism after Aristotle in Peripatetic and Stoic thought before considering the afterlife of Aristotle?s naturalism in the work of Avicenna, Maimonides, and Thomas Aquinas.

course.title: Journaling Journeys
course.description:
Journaling Journeys: Creative Writing Workshop
Can the world and the word be yours at the same time? How much more can journaling tell us about our own experiences? What does journaling teach us about our own future? How can vulnerability on paper give us strength in real life? Through writing, students will take long walks into their younger selves, walk hand in hand with their growing selves. Students will learn how to deconstruct and reconstruct their own lives and their own worlds, and be in conversation with different texts and arts.

course.title: Knowledge, Mind & Existence
course.description:
Introduction to some of the
central issues regarding the nature of knowledge, the mind and reality. Topics to
be discussed include skepticism, the analysis of knowledge, theories of epistemic
justification, the nature of consciousness and subjectivity, mental causation,
dualism, reductive and non-reductive physicalism, proofs for the existence of God,
and personal identity.

course.title: Sociology of Education
course.description: This course is an introduction to the foundations of and current issues in the sociology of education. In this class, we will look at the structure, practices, content, and outcomes of schooling, in light of their relationships to the wider society in which schools are situated.  We will note the link between schools and societal stratification, discuss the outcomes of schooling and how these outcomes are produced, and consider sociological perspectives on contemporary education reforms. This class counts towards the Social Responsibility Praxis requirement. Over the course of the semester, students spend 40 hours working in partnership with a community organization on a culminating course project.

course.title: Quantitative Research Methods
course.description:
In this course, you will learn about the essential statistical techniques used to analyze quantitative data and get direct experience with data analysis. You will learn to analyze data from actual quantitative datasets used by social scientists ( e.g. GSS, ANES, ISSP). By the end of the course, you will possess the skills to not only identify misus of statistics, but to carry out your own data analyis.

As part of the requirements for this course, you will learn to use Stata, a statistical software package commmonly used in academic, business, and non-profit research.

course.title: Hidden: US & Soviet Colonialism
course.description:
Hidden in Plain Sight: U.S. and Soviet Colonialism
This course examines the United States and the former Soviet Union through the lens of colonialism
and empire. While largely invisible to members of both societies and surprisingly also overlooked by
many social scientists, both the United States and the Soviet Union can readily be understood and
analyzed as versions of colonialism and/or empire. The course will highlight similarities and
differences between the two cases regarding a number of specific dimensions of colonial and
imperial social relations. Readings and sources will include perspectives from Ukraine, Kazahkstan,
and other former Soviet societies and American Indian nations and peoples

course.title: Environmental Sociology
course.description:
Environmental Sociology and Climate Futures

The course will examine human societies and their relationships to nature, with an underlying
focus on the societal causes and implications of climate change. While using a sociological lens,
the course will draw on an interdisciplinary mix of materials to explore different societies and
historical and contemporary relationships to the non-human world. In particular, differences
between Euro-American relations structured by capitalism and diverse North American
Indigenous practices shaped by traditional Indigenous knowledge will be featured. In the context
of current and emergent policies, students will imagine transitions to various possible climate
futures, from a decarbonized extension of the present to degrowth transformations to catastrophic
escapism and ecofascism. We will identify possibilities of, processes for, and challenges facing
the restructuring of society towards sustainable--and specifically post-carbon--futures. In
conjunction with the above material, students will be asked to be attentive to their own
relationship with the natural world and to the reality of climate change. I will strive to make the
class a site of mutual support for conscious efforts of self-care in the context of ongoing climate
change.

course.title: Nuclear Culture & Envir. Justice
course.description: This interdisciplinary course explores the cultural, political, and socioenvironmental dimensions of the nuclear age in Latin America. Following the nuclear cycle-from uranium extraction and energy production to radioactive contamination and waste-we examine how nuclear technologies expose human and other-than-human life to radiation, producing "death worlds" in which harms are unevenly distributed along lines of gender, race, ethnicity, and class. Course meets Race and Ethnic Studies general education requirement.

course.title: Figure Drawing and Anatomy
course.description:
This course will focus on drawing as it applies to
the human form. Students will gain a comprehensive knowledge of surface anatomy
and render it correctly. Exercises will include gesture drawing, anatomical studies
and longer poses for value studies. Prerequisite: Drawing 11 or equivalent. Program
fee: $60.

course.title: Drawing
course.description: This class will focus on realism as a basis for accurately perceiving shape, form, value and texture. The course will begin with measuring techniques and perspective, address light and surface quality and end with portraiture. Students will experience a range of drawing media and practice multiple techniques for applying value.

course.title: Research Methods in Polit Stdies
course.description:
This course explores the methods
employed in political studies research. The to primary goals of the course are: 1) to
provide new analytic tools that will help in the critical evaluation of social science
material; and 2) to improve students ability to pose and answer research questions
on their own.

course.title: Intro to Comparative Politics
course.description: This introductory course focuses on explaining political events and processes - like civil war, regime change, revolution, and development - that we regularly read and hear about in the news. Empirically, the course deals with a variety of countries, including those in which Pitzer has study abroad and international exchange programs.

course.title: International Law
course.description: This introduction to core principles of international law examines the rules governing relations among states and other global actors including international organizations. International politics takes place in a context of rules that are increasingly important in a rapidly changing and interconnected world. Where do these rules come from? Do states respect them? And can states be punished for breaking them? We will explore the role these rules play in maintaining order and peace in the international system and addressing issues like territorial conflicts, the use of armed force, international human rights, international migration and refugees, the environment, and international crimes. Prerequisite: GOVT020  CM.

course.title: Intro to Int'l Politics (Honors)
course.description: This course is designed to provide a more in-depth look at international politics for students who have already demonstrated exceptional interest in the topic, academic facility, and initiative. In the first half of the semester, through an interactive, cooperative approach to breaking down questions related to The Commons, you will be introduced to theories and paradigms as well as international relations issues, dilemmas, challenges, structures, and dynamics.  In the second half of the semester, CMC IR professors will guest lecture on their various expertise. By semesterâ¬"s end, you should have familiarity with current world events, some facility with IR theories, an understanding of how the disciplineâ¬"s theories are formed and what they reflect, and a stronger sense of the many variables that influence and explain global politics.

course.title: Chinese Politics
course.description: This course provides an overview of China's political system. It begins with a brief historical overview of China's political development since 1949. The remainder of the course examines the institutional features of the current political system and the key challenges facing the CCP leadership focusing on the prospects of political reform. By applying concepts and theories in comparative politics, we will investigate important issues in Chinese politics, including political selection, state-business relations, protests movements, political participation, public opinion, and media and Internet control. Although students are recommended to have taken comparative politics, there are no prerequisites for this course.

course.title: Nat'lism Populism & Social Media
course.description: Social media plays an important role in comteporary politics. And all around the world, we see the resurgence of populist politicians and political movements. Many of these politicians are master users of the tools of social media, and the movements seem to thrive particularly well in the new media environment. This course explores this interelationship through an exploration of nationalism, an older political ideology that likewise benefited from, and mastered a then-new media enviroment (of newspaper, radio, and television). Is our current digital media-fueled populist moment unique, or are we reproducing an older more durable pattern?

course.title: Law and Politics
course.description:
This course examines the intersection of law,
politics, and policy in the American context. Combining normative and empirical
approaches, we will investigate theories of statutory interpretation, the opportunities
and pitfalls of legal advocacy, the relationship between litigation and legislation,
and the nature of judicial policy-making. Pre-requisites: PS 60 or 10a (or other
intro policy or intro to American politics course) or permission of instructor.

course.title: Power and Social Change
course.description:
Power to the people! Knowledge is power. Taking power. What exactly does one mean by power and how may altering power relations lead to social change? This course will critically examine different theories of power, the relationship between power and violence and how power can be used to liberate as well as dominate and manipulate. This course introduces students to interdisciplinary fields and movements, such as Marxism, feminism, postmodernism,
anti-colonial and postcolonial movements and grassroots movements.

course.title: Environ & Development in 3rd Wld
course.description:
The course explores
the dynamics of positive and/or negative relationships between environment and
development in the Third World. Its theoretical perspectives are complimented by an
experiential requirement in which the students will occasionally visit the maquiladora
enterprises along the U.S./Mexico border.

course.title: Senior Seminar
course.description:
Global Capitalism in Question

This seminar will explore globalization and its impact on the Third World. The course will discuss the various interdisciplinary perspectives on the nature of globalization and the consequences (positive and negative) on the developmental policies and strategies in Third World societies. The discussions will center on the relationships
among economic, political and social-cultural issues, at national, regional and transnational levels. The seminar is designed for seniors in IIS, Political Studies and Economics.

course.title: Global Peace and Conflicts
course.description:
This course examines the nature of global peace and conflicts/wars in the age of globalized world. Broadly, it focuses on
some key and critical theoretical and practical questions, namely, the explanations of the nature of global peace and
conflicts/ wars, and what factors may contribute to practical achievement of peace and security in an interconnected world.
Analyses of case studies are utilized, as well as probing the old and the new global challenges, such as, technologies of
new deadly weapon systems, climate change, widening global income gap, role of religion and gender, among others.

course.title: Hist & Globalization of Football
course.description:
History and Globalization of Football	
This course examines topics in the history and politics of world soccer. We will see how culture, politics and history play themselves out upon the stage of stadium and field, from fascist Italy to indomitable Cameroon.  We will see how the World Cup has become a catalyst for political and cultural debate, and how it has made, and undermined, political regimes. And we will try to understand the game as others, in different times and places, have seen it: a game freighted with meaning and beauty.

course.title: Reinforcement Learning
course.description: Reinforcement learning (RL) is the problem of a decision-making agent in an unfamiliar environment that receives some reward/punishment signal about its behavior. The agent's goal is to learn from experience to make decisions that obtain more reward. This course will consider this problem from a computational perspective, with the aim of understanding mathematical formalizations of the RL problem, computational challenges posed by the problem, and algorithmic approaches to addressing some of those challenges. Topics will include fundamental challenges, including temporal credit assignment and exploration vs. exploitation; foundational algorithms; modern RL techniques, including deep reinforcement learning; and additional advanced topics as time permits. Prerequisite: MATH151.

course.title: Integrated Sci Research II
course.description: In this 0.5-credit course, students will gain experience working independently on an Integrated Sciences research experience, which may involve field, laboratory, or computational research (or any combination thereof) and will be mentored by a KDIS faculty member.  The format and expectations of the research will be mutually agreed upon at the start of the semester and must include an end-of-semester deliverable (e.g., reflection paper, oral or poster presentation, lab notebook, dataset, etc.). This course is a 0.5-credit course with a minimum of a 6-hour commitment each week. The course is taken as pass/fail. A total of at most 1 credit may accumulate in SCI196 and SCI197 towards graduation. The course may not be counted toward major requirements. In any semester, students may take only one Integrated Sciences Research course at KDIS.  Prerequisite: Permission of instructor

course.title: Compar Environmental Politics
course.description:
An examination of the political challenges faced by environmental advocates in diverse countries around the globe. Drawing on the fields of comparative politics and public policy, topics include comparative political institutions, environmental movements, corruption, authoritarian regimes, democratization, lesson-learning across borders, policy reform, gender analysis, decentralization and European unification.

HSA Writing Intensive: No

course.title: History of Design
course.description: History of design starting with the Industrial Revolution through issues shaping design in the 21st century. Emphasis will be placed on the design movements that emerged globally in the 19th and 20th century. Design is a social phenomenon, and we will pay close attention to the artistic, cultural, political, and technological factors that influence design, and how design, in turn, shapes society.

course.title: Human Relationships with Lab
course.description: This course will explore how social relationships shape human development across the life course. We will take an interdisciplinary view of human relationships, drawing on developmental and evolutionary psychology, social neuroscience, anthropology, and health sciences. Topics include parent-child attachment across cultures, peer relationships and friendship formation, romantic relationships, loneliness, physiological effects of touch, and the impacts of relationship quality on physical and mental health during different developmental periods. Lab will focus on research methods in relationship science, experimental and observational approaches, and an introduction to dyadic and longitudinal data analysis. Students will complete a final project using real-world data on love and social connection.

course.title: Politics of Race and Ethnicity
course.description: This course will examine critical questions and debates in race, ethnicity, and politics. It utilizes a multi-disciplinary approach to investigate the history of racial and ethnic minorities in the U.S. and examines the interaction of minority politics within broader American politics. The course begins with theoretical conceptions of race and ethnicity and how they inform notions of citizenship, group membership, structural racism, and racial hierarchies. Subsequent topics include voting and redistricting, electoral politics, segregation and discrimination, social movements, and cooperation and competition within and among minority groups. Finally, selected contemporary policy issues and practices will be discussed in light of their impact on minority communities such as criminal justice, education, health care, and environmental policy. Prerequisites: POLI003  PO or PPA 001  PO. Previously offered as POLI045  PO.

course.title: Legal Histories of Empire
course.description: This course examines some of the myriad ways in which the modern British and French empires were made and contested through law. It considers the role of imperial administrators in developing and imposing laws and legal concepts, as well as the agency of local actors in negotiating imperial legal regimes. Utilizing case studies covering commercial, criminal, and family law among other categories, the course will be particularly attentive to the way in which imperial power worked in intimate, local, regional and transnational contexts, and to the cross-cutting impacts of race, class, and gender.

course.title: Mexican Modernism
course.description: This course explores the vibrant flourishing of art in early twentieth-century Mexico. It is organized around the study of paintings, prints, photographs, and murals by artists including Diego Rivera, José Clemente Orozco, Frida Kahlo, and Tina Modotti, as well as artist statements, manifestos, and art criticism. We will study how artists engaged nation-building programs, incorporated the aesthetic values of indigenous and Afro-descendent peoples, and challenged colonial notions of race, gender, and class. And we will follow the modernists into the world and to the Claremont Colleges, home to two famous works of Mexican muralism in the United States.

course.title: Mughal Art and Architecture
course.description: This seminar focuses on the art and architecture of the Mughal empire (1526-1857). It explores monuments such as the Taj Mahal; the Mughal capitals at Agra, Delhi, and Lahore; paintings, manuscripts, and albums; textiles; and courtly and luxury objects. The course addresses a range of topics, including patronage, artistic agency, religiosity, cultural encounter, and the natural environment. It takes a transhistorical perspective, considering the ongoing influence of Mughal visual culture in popular culture and in the practice of contemporary artists. It also takes a transregional perspective, comparing the Mughals with contemporary powers from Europe and Turkey to Iran and China.

course.title: Classical Buddhist Philosophy
course.description:
While Buddhism is a religious tradition with the goal of spiritual liberation from suffering, it was also, from its origin in Ancient India 2500 years ago, a philosophical attempt to understand reality, the mind, and the meaning of life. In this course, we will address Buddhism as philosophy, rather than as a religious practice. 

We will, therefore, begin by exploring the central philosophical arguments attributed to the historical Buddha as well as the more systematic metaphysical, epistemological, and ethical theories of Abhidharma period Buddhism. We will then proceed to examine the development of Mah?y?na Buddhism, including Yog?c?ra and Madhyamaka. After which we will consider Tibetan Madhyamaka and Chinese Buddhist schools, including the Chinese Yog?c?ra, Chan, Tiantai, and Huayan, along with the Japanese Zen school. Finally, we will consider modern interpretations of Buddhist philosophy, including socially engaged Buddhism.

course.title: Fútbol, Mundo, Barrio y Pícaros
course.description: In this course we will examine the cultural commons of Football in the Hispanophone world. By attending to different medium modes, such as but not limited to; football history, film, game archives, visual art, music, and journalism, we will analyze, both, how discriminatory power structures such as FIFA, function, and how localized styles of play and club teams serve as a space where contestations and resistances take place. Through careful and critical focus on cultural manifestations, contextualized by relevant readings in cultural studies, sports studies and critical theory, we will re-examine what ?fair-play? is in the context of the sport and FIFA, considering the varied expressive cultures that constitute the game, within and adjacent to the Hispanophone world.

course.title: Art of Attention
course.description: This is a course about attention-- paying it, using it, cultivating it, and keeping it. Forms of research include historical, critical, and spiritual texts; direct observation; writing; strolling; sitting; listening; and analog photographic processes. Students will work together to create and maintain an attention sanctuary, within which we will spend the semester collectively studying and practicing our attentions, with the goal of understanding how an artistic practice might benefit from habits of attention. Projects include the creation of photographs and an attention journal. This class requires slowing down, experimentation, and the willingness to attend.

course.title: Research Methods
course.description: This course provides an overview of issues related to the conduct of psychological inquiry. Topics to be covered include measurement, research design (observational, experimental and survey approaches) and research ethics. Psychology 92 is designed to be taken after Psychology 91 and is well-suited for sophomores. This course does not replace Psychology 112,which must be taken by seniors carrying out thesis projects. Prerequisites: Psychology 10 and Psychology 91.

course.title: Context Shapes Behavior
course.description: This course will focus on how the same sensory stimulus in different contexts can produce highly flexible and opposite behavioral responses on various time scales. We will explore the molecular, cellular, and neural mechanisms that encode flexible behavior.  Examples will be drawn from invertebrate and vertebrate sensory systems. Emphasis is placed on critically evaluating readings from the primary literature, leading scientific discussion, designing experiments, and producing clear scientific writing.

course.title: Research Methods Practicum
course.description: This lab course will provide students with hands-on experience in research design and methodology in the field of psychology. Students will get experience in all phases of the research process (i.e., conducting a literature search, designing a study, collecting and analyzing data, and writing up APA-style reports).

course.title: Collage
course.description: This course focuses on creating collages and montages, from analog to digital and from 2D to 3D to 4D. As part of the creative process, students will explore the history of collage, from its radical and revolutionary origins in the early 20th century to contemporary applications. Throughout the semester there will be opportunities to work individually and collaboratively, and students will be challenged to think expansively and push the boundaries of what is possible with compositing, juxtapositions and blurred ideas of authorship. $50 course materials fee.

course.title: Contemporary Solid State Physics
course.description:
Fundamental ideas and principles in solid state physics, including lattice structure, lattice excitations, and the motion and excitations of electrons in metals. Models of electronic states of matter, including metals, insulators, and semiconductors, magnetism, and superconductivity. Added emphasis on connections to contemporary research areas. Lectures and student-led seminar presentations. Interested students who have previously taken Physics 162 should consult with the instructors. 
Prerequsite: PHYS117  HM. Corequisite: PHYS116  HM.

course.title: Major Issues in Foreign Policy
course.description: This course is designed to give students an opportunity to examine historical and contemporary issues in American foreign policy with an appreciation for the diplomatic and military instruments of national power. The course is broken into three parts. Part I emphasizes bureaucratic politics and the institutional interests within the State Department and Pentagon, including interagency policymaking and the National Security Council staff. Part II explores historical case studies that illustrate American attempts to employ diplomacy and coercive military force in tandem. Part III presents contemporary cases that address U.S. national security challenges through diplomatic and military means, with an emphasis on America's global competitors.

course.title: Logistics and Counter-logistics
course.description: The word "logistics" is often shorthand for the boring, tedious, and largely invisibilized details of everyday life, the background noise of our needs, wants, tastes, and desires. Yet as we careen from one global crisis to another, these systems move from background to foreground. We are all increasingly aware of the subterranean layer that undergirds the movement (and non-movement) of people, commodities, information across disparate geographies. This class will attune students to the political, social, and affective arrangements of logistical life. The class will consider "the logistics" of empire, the state, and capitalism, but also "logistics from below" as practiced by insurgents, activists, pilgrims, smugglers, migrants, and other more and less subaltern actors. More than considering logistics and counter-logistics as antagonists, the course will consider how these categories collaborate.

course.title: Child Development
course.description:
Evidence pertaining to the development of the child is
examined and discussed in relation to selected theoretical formulations. Facets of
the childs cognitive, social, emotional and personality development are included.
Enrollment is limited.

course.title: Programming Interactivity
course.description: In this class, students will write interactive programs in a variety of paradigms, ranging from simple command-line tools to graphical applications and videogames.  We will pay special attention to how the way we understand user interaction nudges us into structuring our program along particular lines.

course.title: Social Science of Toxicity
course.description: What makes something toxic, polluted, or contaminated, and how do social, political, economic, and historical processes shape how we understand and experience these conditions? This course examines contamination, pollution, toxicity, and exposure through interdisciplinary approaches from the social sciences, environmental studies, and the humanities. We will examine how societies define and measure environmental harm, and how these concepts offer different ways of understanding environmental conditions, social relations, and inequalities. Drawing on scholarship from anthropology, sociology, political ecology, and science and technology studies, students will examine the relationships among scientific knowledge, environmental regulation, industrial development, labor, colonialism, and inequality. We will consider how toxic substances move through landscapes and bodies, how different forms of exposure are understood and regulated, and how communities respond to environmental harm.

course.title: Introduction to Archaeology
course.description: This class introduces students to Archaeology. It surveys its history, politics, and contributions to our understanding of the world. It also introduces students to the strengths and weaknesses of archaeological theory and methods. Finally, it explores archaeology's unique insights into historical processes and contexts. Students will learn when and how a focus on material culture could enhance their own analyses of the worlds they live in and hope to build.

course.title: Sex, Body and Reproduction
course.description: Is there a line between nature and culture? Drawing on historical, ethnographic and popular sources, this course will examine the cultural roots of forms of knowledge about sex, the body and reproduction and the circulation of cultural metaphors in medical, historical and colonial discourse.

course.title: Geological Field Methods
course.description: Introduction to the fundamental skills and techniques used to investigate Earth materials, landforms, and geological processes in the field. Students apply field methods, including geological mapping and data collection, to investigate and interpret the geology of a study area. Two field trips.

course.title: Numerical Models in Volcanology
course.description: This semester, via reading, class discussions and hands-on learning you will gain an introduction to how and why numerical models are used to investigate geological problems. Our specific focus will be learning to use finite element method (FEM) techniques as we explore a few different key mechanical and thermal processes in volcanology.

course.title: Intro Sociocultural Anthropology
course.description: An introduction to the basic concepts, theories and methods of social and cultural anthropology. An investigation of the nature of sociocultural systems using ethnographic materials from a wide range of societies.

course.title: Ancient Race and Ethnicity
course.description: How did ancient Greeks and Romans construct categories of racial and ethnic difference? What do literary and material sources reveal about the lived experiences of enslaved peoples, foreigners, and (non)citizen populations in antiquity? How have modern scholarly traditions and popular narratives reinforced or challenged these ancient frameworks? To develop answers to these questions we will conduct an ancient-text-based and theoretically-informed exploration of race, ethnicity, and human difference in Greek and Latin literature, alongside visual and material culture from across the Mediterranean. We will examine how Classics has historically participated in colonial and exclusionary practices, and how it is being reinterpreted today. By engaging with primary sources, analyzing scholarship, and reflecting on contemporary implications, students will become a community of scholars equipped to make rigorous humanistic arguments about identity, belonging, and power in antiquity and today.

course.title: Nature of Work
course.description:
This course explores psychological issues related to the
changing nature of work. With a primary focus on the human side of organizational
life, we will examine how changes in technology, international relations and social
expectations shape present and future understanding of work in our contemporary
world.

course.title: Organizational Behavior
course.description:
We will investigate individual, group and structural
factors that work to influence patterns of behavior in organizations. The course will
incorporate a variety of methods designed to highlight important issues in the field
and students will be expected to work through individual and group projects related
to the area. Prerequisite: Orst 100 and/or Orst/Psyc 103.

course.title: Organizational Life
course.description: This course highlights life in organizations using a variety of theoretical lenses to explore important factors operating in this context. Students will investigate individual, social and societal influences present in organizations and apply knowledge gained from these studies to analyze relevant cases and better understand their own experience.

course.title: Some Versions of The Tempest
course.description: This course will consider Shakespeare's final play, The Tempest, across its long life of adaptation, revision, mutation, and reinterpretation. In some ways, The Tempest has become an aesthetic tradition unto itself. To what uses-- aesthetic, political, philosophical-- has the play been put, and why do artists return so often to it? Adapted three times in its own era, by the twentieth century artists across the globe used The Tempest to address the long legacies of colonialism, race, and slavery; genre and artistry; queerness and gender; and capitalism and its alternatives. Some of the adaptations are faithful, others are startling and unexpected. The diverse transformations point to how much is contained within The Tempest as well as what the original play cannot address. We will begin and end with Shakespeare's Tempest; in between, we will consider its adaptations in different media including opera, animation, poetry, philosophy, film, and fiction.

course.title: Social Identity
course.description: This course explores how group memberships become part of our identities and how social identities influence how we think, feel, and behave. Grounded in social identity theory, we will examine foundational principles of social identity as well as applications and extensions of this framework (e.g., well-being, echo chambers, prosocial behavior, social protests, schisms, leadership). Students will engage with classic and contemporary research to understand how social identities can contribute to both positive outcomes, such as belonging and cooperation, and negative outcomes, such as intergroup bias and conflict.

course.title: Adv Speech & Rhetoric: Debate
course.description:
Advanced Speech and Rhetoric: Argument & Debate 

Students will critique and present arguments in formal spoken English through debates, discussions and extemporaneous talks centered around contemporary issues. Models of argumentation will be analyzed. Letter grades only. Written permission required.

course.title: Topics in Phil of Neuroscience
course.description: This seminar is an examination of selected issues at the intersection of contemporary philosophy and neuroscience. Topics may include the metaphysical relationship between the mind and the brain; the nature of theory, evidence, and explanation in neuroscience (and how neuroscience relates to other cognitive sciences); the neuroscience of freedom of the will; the physical basis of cognition in the brain, as well as how neuroscientific explanations comport with commonsense notions of the self and moral responsibility.

course.title: Game Theory with Public Policy A
course.description: Why do rational individuals produce outcomes that make everyone worse off, and what can policy do about it? This course introduces game theory through hands-on classroom experiments and applies it to externalities, public goods, financial panics, asymmetric information, political economy, and international agreements. Students learn to model strategic situations, solve for equilibria, and evaluate policy responses such as carbon taxes, cap-and-trade, deposit insurance, and mandates

course.title: Plague and Literature
course.description: How has literature depicted widespread illness, and what can we learn from literary representations of epidemics? How have ideas about disease connected to theories of happiness, suffering, sex, loss, justice, law, the divine, the environment, medical treatment, civilization, the state, and the future? Authors we read in this introductory course may include Sophocles, Thucydides, Boccaccio, Defoe, Poe, Chekhov, Mann, Camus, McNeill, Girard, Sontag, Sorokin, Kushner, Whitehead, Smith, and Mandel.

course.title: Fund of Autonomous Robotics
course.description: This course introduces the fundamental principles of mobile robotics, emphasizing robot motion, control, localization, mapping, and autonomous navigation. Topics include coordinate transformations, robot kinematics, motion control, robot localization, and path-planning algorithms such as Dijkstras algorithm, A\* search, and probabilistic roadmaps. Students will learn the fundamentals of Python-based robotics programming and gain hands-on experience in developing and implementing robotic applications. Prerequisite: ENGR101  HM.

course.title: Readings in Islamic Philosophy
course.description:
This course introduces students to the fundamental concepts and problems of Islamic philosophy in the classical period (ca. 850?1250). How did Muslims philosophers justify philosophical inquiry? What did they have to say about perennial questions like free will and predestination, proof of God's existence, the origins of the universe, or the way to attain happiness? How did issues particular to Islam-- monotheism, prophecy, and divine law-- affect how Muslims approached the study of philosophy? This course is not a survey but will rather consist in the close reading and discussion of primary sources in translation. Readings might include texts by al-Farabi, Ibn Sina, al-Juwayni, and Ibn Tufayl. 

This course does not require any previous knowledge of or experience with Islam, philosophy, or religious studies. Students of all levels are welcome.

course.title: Arts of Spain and Spanish World
course.description: This class provides an introduction to the visual culture of Spain and the Spanish world. The course begins with medieval Iberia and ends in the first two decades of the nineteenth century. The following subjects will be explored: the circulation and development of Islamic art and architecture in Iberia; the plurality of visual forms shaped by cultural coexistence; the deployment of images during Spain?s age of exploration; the relationship between vision, spirituality, and pictorial representation; and the aesthetics of the modern in nineteenth-century Spain and Spanish America.

course.title: Contemporary Caribbean Art
course.description: This seminar course explores contemporary Caribbean photography, performance, experimental film, video, and installation. Through weekly themes, students will engage with the different mediums, organized around form, technique, and modes of inquiry. Students will read scholarly and creative texts alongside visual work to understand the historical and contemporary contexts from which the works emerge. Students will examine how constructs around "paradise," islands, marronage, transatlantic slavery and the plantation, multiculturalism, postcolonialism, spirituality, Blackness, gender, and queerness shape aesthetic approaches and visual expression across this complex and ever-evolving region.

course.title: Perspectives on Rationality
course.description: This course explores perspectives on human rationality from several disciplines, including psychology, economics, and philosophy.  How can "rationality" be defined?  And what does psychological research tell us about the rationality, or irrationality, of human judgment and decision making?  We will examine formal models of rationality, considering their strengths and limitations, and ask to what extent rational models do, or don't, provide useful descriptions of human behavior.

course.title: Latino Politics
course.description: This course will cover the historical background of the group, identity formation, political participation and collective action among the various subgroups that comprise the Latino/a/e demographic. Additionally, we will discuss the issues that shape the group's political behaviors such as immigration, racial discrimination, and voting rights. This class will also focus on the relationship between the Latino/a/e community and other racialized groups in the U.S. to better understand how institutional barriers limit political participation for marginalized communities.

course.title: Anthropology of Im/migration
course.description: Migration is a defining political question and pivotal human experience of the contemporary world. Centering movement between Latin America and the United States, with comparative cases of asylum and humanitarian aid in Europe and Africa, this course takes an anthropological approach to migration. How do borders, passports, and legal status govern human movement? How are terms like "illegal," "refugee," and "immigrant" produced by law and politics? What do they mean for people's work, health, and family lives? Combining ethnography, history, and media analysis, students will engage with subjects such as border enforcement, labor, detention and deportation, cultural belonging, transnational families, undocumented youth, and humanitarianism.

course.title: The Transmitted Image
course.description: This course considers photography?s foundational role within the conceptual art movement by exploring a longer pre-history of photography?s intertwined relations with communications media. Almost as soon as inventors discovered techniques for fixing images onto plates or paper negatives in the early 19th century, makers focused their attention on how to circulate photographs, from lapel pins to book-like daguerreotype cases. Later, in the 1930s, the Associated Press launched a  ?wire photo? service, which transmitted photographic prints via electronic signals over the radio or telephone wires, raising questions about how images are manipulated. We will explore wire photographs from the civil rights movement; the global ?mail art? movement; and the emergence of Conceptual Art in the 1970s. This course will be taught in conjunction with exhibitions and events taking place at the Benton Museum of Art.

course.title: Advanced Fiction Workshop
course.description: This is an intensive writing workshop for advanced fiction writers, those who have longer stories or a booklength project, this is a great class for you. This is also a good course for those working on a creative senior thesis. We will meet weekly to discuss one another's writing in progress. Occasional supplemental readings. Prerequisite: a creative writing course or introductory fiction course, or commiserate experience with writing sample to receive permission.By the end of this course you will have bravely and extensively revised 3000 of 5000 words of prose, and written one original 10-12 pages of fiction.

course.title: Interpersonal Relationships
course.description: Interpersonal Relationships.  This seminar course and its paired practicum course provide a selective review of psychological theory and research on interpersonal relationships, with particular emphasis on social psychological approaches and findings.  Through a variety of readings and class discussions, along with some lectures and other activities, the processes and dynamics of interpersonal relationships will be explored.

course.title: Interpersonal Relationships Prac
course.description: This seminar course and its paired practicum course provide a selective review of psychological theory and research on interpersonal relationships, with particular emphasis on social psychological approaches and findings.  Through a variety of readings and class discussions, along with some lectures and other activities, the processes and dynamics of interpersonal relationships will be explored.

course.title: Music and Nationalism
course.description: *No musical background is required for success in this course.* Following the victories of the first nationalist movements in the late 18th century, the nation-state rapidly became the world's primary mode of political organization. Even today, though, definitions of the nation-state remain notoriously elusive. 21st-century scholars continue to debate question like, "What is a nation?," "Where do nations come from?," and "Who belongs to a nation?" Despite the many outstanding questions, it is clear that cultural productsliterature, theater, the plastic arts, and musicplay a significant role in all nationalisms. In this class, we will focus on music as a means of understanding how nations are formed, sustained, and contested. Drawing on a set of interdisciplinary readings, we will explore the theoretical foundations of nations and nationalism, and the ways that national imaginaries interact with some of the defining issues of the modern world, including colonialism, globalism, race, totalitarianism, and democracy. We will supplement these theoretical readings with listenings from across the globe. Regions covered in this course have included cases as varied as the US, the Dominican Republic, Zimbabwe, and China.

course.title: PopMusEastAsia: Political&SocHis
course.description: *No background in music is required to succeed in this course.* This course investigates the social and political circumstances that gave rise to East Asian popular music. Drawing on a broad array of scholarship on the popular music of East Asia, focusing on China, Japan, Korea, and Taiwan, we begin with the earliest examples of East Asian popular music from the early 20th century, and explore the effect of changing political and social conditions on the popular music of the region from the early 20th century until today. Students will be introduced to a variety of methods for engaging with the history, aesthetics, and social significance of popular music from this region. Throughout the course, we will not only listen to and watch a wide variety of popular musics, we will also ask what it means for music to be "popular."

course.title: Global Leadership
course.description:
Global Leadership looks at world historical events through the lens of social change by decentering the political
to reflect its transnational context. Students will consider the efforts of individuals and networks to enact vital and
positive change in the world. Moreso than nations, the site of this leadership often rested in international
institutions intergovernmental or non-governmental. The course materials reveal developments in alternative
discourses; evaluations of the global economy and its determining factors and inequalities; the sexual and the
geographical divisions of labor; humanitarianism and transnational activism; and the ongoing negotiation
surrounding international norms and behaviors.

course.title: Brain and Behavior
course.description: This course provides an introduction to the biological bases of cognition and behavior. Topics may include basic neurophysiology, neuroanatomy, visual and auditory perception, attention, language, hemispheric specialization, memory, emotion, motor control, and social neuroscience. Satisfies: BIO.

course.title: Writing with AI
course.description:
Writing with AI: Evolution, Impact, and Ethics
Artificial Intelligence in Education (AIED) has been around as early as the 1950s, supporting neurodivergent students and students with physical accessibility needs in the classroom. As AI progressed from the first typewriter to computers and smart devices, today, AI is changing the way we engage with the writing process and written communication. From narrow AI such as Siri and Alexa to generative AI and Large Language Models (LLMs) like ChatGPT and Gemini, educators are increasingly grappling with the ethical implications of writing in a world with AI. This class continues the discussion of AI, particularly LLMs, and its evolutionary approaches to writing. What does writing look like in a world of AI? What is the role of LLMs? How can LLMs support or hinder the writing process? What are the long-term and ethical implications of LLMs and AI with writing? In this activity-based seminar, students will apply the different forms of generative AI and LLMs and develop the necessary skills to determine whether AI and LLMs should be regulated in the classroom or workplace and if so, how.

course.title: Lang and Community:Teaching ESL
course.description:
This course will introduce students to the theory and practice of teaching English as
a second language within the context of the local community of Southern California.
The main focus of the course will be teaching adults basic English, the language
necessary to live and work successfully within the community.

course.title: Statistics
course.description:
An introduction to the statistical tools used in the quantitative
analysis of economic and political relationships. Topics include probability theory,
statistical estimation, hypothesis testing and regression analysis. Prerequisite:
ECON051 or ECON52

course.title: Principles of Microeconomics
course.description: Principles of Microeconomics is an introductory course that teaches the fundamentals of microeconomics.  This course introduces microeconomic concepts and analysis including consumer choice by individuals, price and output decisions by firms under various market structures, supply and demand analysis in product and labor markets, welfare outcomes for consumers and producers, the effects of government taxes and policies, market efficiency ad market failure, and income distribution.  We rely heavily on analysis using a graphical representation, though also discuss how these formal concepts apply to real-world issues.

course.title: Principles of Microeconomics
course.description: Principles of Microeconomics is an introductory course that teaches the fundamentals of microeconomics.  This course introduces microeconomic concepts and analysis including consumer choice by individuals, price and output decisions by firms under various market structures, supply and demand analysis in product and labor markets, welfare outcomes for consumers and producers, the effects of government taxes and policies, market efficiency ad market failure, and income distribution.  We rely heavily on analysis using a graphical representation, though also discuss how these formal concepts apply to real-world issues.

course.title: Intro Sociocultural Anthropology
course.description: An introduction to the basic concepts, theories and methods of social and cultural anthropology. An investigation of the nature of sociocultural systems using ethnographic materials from a wide range of societies.

course.title: Participatory Action Research
course.description: More than a methodology, Participatory Action Research (PAR) is a model of inquiry for emancipatory social change, prioritizing the wisdom and aspirations of those closest to unequal and harmful social systems. This course gives students practice doing community-driven research that is specifically designed to address a local need, support local initiatives, and amplify local innovations. To resist the extractive and transactional tendencies in all of us, PAR requires a high level of self-awareness, interdependence, and accountability, as well as acceptance of the beautiful messiness of grassroots work on the ground. This semester, small teams of students will be partnered with local organizations to support their efforts at fundraising and grant writing. The course will also include a global module in which students will engage with Pitzer's community partners in Ecuador and with experts on the political and economic challenges facing global grassroots organizations in our current times of economic precarity, funding cuts, crisis in US international assistance, and the Trump administration's rejection of foreign aid and embrace of militarism.

course.title: RaceGender&Class:GreatRecession
course.description: The December 2007 collapse of the U.S. housing and financial markets brought about the worst economic crisis (to date) since the Great Depression. This course will investigate the underpinnings, asymmetrical consequences, and long afterlives of the Great Recession, beginning from the American studies premise that its economic dimensions are inseparable from its social, cultural, affective, and (geo)political ones. Together, we will grapple with reactionary political and aesthetic responses to what Ruth Wilson Gilmore calls "organized abandonment" and explore the alternatives offered by progressive social movements, artists, and critics seeking to reintroduce the language of class and (geo)political economy (and their crucial imbrications with race and gender) more clearly into U.S. political, academic, and cultural discourse.

course.title: Architecture on Display
course.description: This course explores the history of architectural display from the 17th century to present day. Putting architecture on display is one of the most widely enacted and fundamental aspects of critical contemporary architecture, as evidenced by the recent of wave of pavilions, installations, exhibitions, and biennales. As a practice, display makes public (and sometimes evident) architecture itself, including its meanings and definitions, but it also produces other architectures: the cabinet of curiosities, the urban procession, the house museum, the period room, the white modernist cube, the full-scale mock-up, the computational media room, the site-specific installation, the temporary pavilion, and the digital interface. As such, when architecture is put on display, it also produces new architectures and is thus a mode of production. This course will explore historic episodes of exhibition architecture in order to understand what was displayed, as well as how such objects, artifacts, and works were displayed. By examining the media, techniques, instruments and circumstances that paralleled architectural production in order to unveil it, the course hopes to expand on the idea of exhibition-making to be not only a practice of presentation but also a mode of critical production. From historic case studies such as Lenoirs Museum of Monuments to John Soanes house museum, to more recent tendencies including the pavilion phenomenon and the Chicago Biennale, each weeks topics and readings will begin to unpack the ways architecture produces and is produced by its own display.

course.title: Social Documentation/Asian-Amer
course.description: Viewing of films and other documentary forms by Asian Americans and Pacific Islanders (AAPI) for critique and discussion. Basic instruction in use of digital video technology to document social issues relevant to Asian American and Pacific Islander communities. Community-project.

course.title: Introduction to Astrophysics
course.description: A general survey of modern astrophysics. Topics covered include electromagnetic radiation, gravitation, stellar structure and evolution, the interstellar medium and the birth of stars, supernovae and the death of stars (including the physics of neutron stars and black holes), synthesis of the elements, and the formation, structure and evolution of galaxies and of the universe. Prerequisite: Physics 51. Offered jointly with Pomona and Joint Sciences.

course.description: Application of molecular biology techniques to problems in human genetics, bioengineering, and environmental sensing. Fall and Spring.

course.description: Topics in ecology, evolution, molecular genetics, and computational biology. Corequisite: CSCI005  HM or CSCI042  HM.

course.description: Investigations in physiology, biochemistry, ecology, molecular biology and other areas of experimental biology. Corequisite: (Biology 23 and Biology 46). Concurrent requisite: Biology 154.

course.description: Investigations in physiology, biochemistry, ecology, molecular biology and other areas of experimental biology. Corequisite: (Biology 23 and Biology 46). Concurrent requisite: Biology 154.

course.title: Comparative Physiology
course.description: The general aim will provide a broad introduction to comparative physiology. Students will learn the links between cellular & molecular mechanisms, organ systems, and organismal function in animals. Students will examine the relationship between structure and function in biology. During the process, students will be introduced to the diversity of animals and the scientific tools used to make physiological measurements. Prerequisite: BIOL046  HM.

course.title: Ecology & Environmental Biology
course.description: Principles of organization of natural communities and ecosystems, including population dynamics, species interactions, and island biogeography. Modern experimental and mathematical approaches to ecological problems. Application of ecological principles to conservation biology, climate change, and other environmental impacts. Prerequisites: Biology 46 and Mathematics 19.

course.title: Biostatistics
course.description: Statistical techniques for analyzing biological data, including parametric, nonparametric, and randomization methods. Statistical aspects of experimental design with an emphasis on analyzing data collected in Biology 54. Prerequisites: (Computer Science 5, 5GR, or 42). Corequisite: Biology 46. Concurrent registration in Biology 54 required.

course.title: Research Problems in Biology
course.description: Original experimental investigations in biology undertaken in consultation with a faculty member. (May not be counted for credit toward the Biology major.) Prerequisite: Permission of instructor. 1-3 credit hours. 1 credit hour for each 3 hours of research per week.

course.title: Biochemistry
course.description: Relation of molecular structure and energy flow to reactions in living systems. Prerequisite: Chemistry 56  and Junior/Senior Standing. (Crosslisted as CHEM182  HM).

course.title: Biochemistry Laboratory
course.description: Experiments in biochemistry. Corequisite: Biology/Chemistry 182 (may be taken concurrently). (Crosslisted as CHEM184  HM)

course.title: Biology Colloquium
course.description: Oral presentations and discussions of selected topics including recent developments. Participants include biology majors, faculty members and visiting speakers. Required for junior and senior biology majors. No more than 2.0 credits of credit can be earned for colloquium.  Pass/No Credit grading. Prerequisite(s): HMC Biology (including joint majors) only.

course.title: Senior Thesis Research: Biology

course.title: Chemistry in the Modern World
course.description: Chemistry plays a powerful role in addressing an array of current and future global and societal challenges. This course examines contemporary applications of chemistry to describe innovative advances in such areas as energy, medicine, technology, materials, to name a few. These applications illustrate such fundamental concepts as molecular and electronic structure in dictating chemical and physical properties; intermolecular forces, phase behavior, thermodynamics, electrochemistry, kinetics, and equilibria. Lecture and individual and group exercises conducted in class are used as a context for introducing chemistry principles. Corequisite(s): CHEM024 HM.

course.title: Computations in Chemistry
course.description: This course introduces students to a wide range of computation tools used in chemistry through computational projects in Python while exploring certain central chemical concepts. Topics include the basics of quantum chemistry orbital calculations, molecular simulations of liquids and biochemical systems, cheminformatics, and the use of programming to study chemical reactions and model chemical systems. Besides exposure to computational techniques in chemistry, the students will also deepen their understanding of molecular systems and chemical principles and develop skills in modeling and analysis of complex chemical problems. Prerequisite: CSCI005  HM (or equivalent). Co-requisite: CHEM042  HM.

course.title: Chemical Analysis

course.title: Inorganic Chemistry

course.title: Organic Chemistry II
course.description: This course continues the study of chemical properties and reactions of carbon-containing compounds, with particular emphasis on aromatic systems and carbonyl compounds. The course focuses on developing molecular understanding and problem-solving skills as a foundation for future study in the chemical, biological, and materials sciences. Prerequisite: Chemistry 56. Chemistry 111 should be taken concurrently.

course.title: PhyChem IIA Quantum Chemistry
course.description: We will discuss the foundations of quantum mechanics as applicable to problems in chemistry. The course covers fundamental topics in quantum chemistry: wave-particle duality, solutions to several cases of the Schrodinger Equation, interpretation and rationalization of spectroscopic measurements, and electronic structure calculations. Prerequisite: CHEM051  HM or PHYS051  HM.

course.title: Chem of the Oceans & Atmosphere
course.description: An advanced chemistry course exploring the most important chemical systems of the oceans and atmosphere including ocean acidification and alkalinity, eutrophication, biogeochemical cycling, global climate change, stratospheric ozone, and the chemistry of ground-level air pollution. Includes chemical mechanisms, and thermodynamic and kinetic considerations for these canonical systems. Prerequisites: CHEM051  HM and CHEM056  HM.
