course.title: Public Policy Analysis
course.description: This course provides an introduction to public policy analysis. Drawing on the principles and tools of political science and economics, students will hone their ability to analyze complex public problems. The course uses the case method, immersing students in real-world scenarios and placing them in the role of decision maker. Students will learn to write professional policy memos and to use Excel for basic data analysis.  Cross-listed as ECON 097. Prerequisites: ECON050 and GOVT020.

course.title: Public Policy Analysis
course.description: This course provides an introduction to public policy analysis. Drawing on the principles and tools of political science and economics, students will hone their ability to analyze complex public problems. The course uses the case method, immersing students in real-world scenarios and placing them in the role of decision maker. Students will learn to write professional policy memos and to use Excel for basic data analysis. Cross-listed as GOVT097 CM. Prerequisites: GOVT020 CM and ECON050 CM.

course.title: Spanish Virtual Learning Commnty
course.description:
This course is a virtual learning community for linguistic and cultural exchange in Spanish
and English. You are paired up with a conversation partner abroad with whom you have weekly conversations in Spanish and English. You interact through Zoom or other platforms on your own schedule. In addition, 1 hour debriefing meetings with your instructor every 2 weeks will take place during the scheduled class time. Faculty provide a curricular structure for the exchange, with a scaffolding of activities stressing specific linguistic competencies. There is room for you and your partner abroad
to develop a relationship through meaningful exchanges on topics of shared personal interest (everyday life, music, art sport, social political issues or events as they unfold in
both countries). The purpose of these exchanges is to help you develop confidence and oral proficiency in Spanish and broaden your intercultural understanding from an international perspective. At least two semesters of Spanish or equivalent is required.

course.title: Adv. Spanish: Language & Culture
course.description:
Discussion of texts and/or films concerning literary and social aspects of Spain and
Latin America. Development of correct personal style and/or idiomatic expressions
in oral and written expression. Prerequisite: Spanish 33, placement examination or
equivalent.

course.title: Adv. Spanish: Language & Culture
course.description:
Discussion of texts and/or films concerning literary and social aspects of Spain and
Latin America. Development of correct personal style and/or idiomatic expressions
in oral and written expression. Prerequisite: Spanish 33, placement examination or
equivalent.

course.title: Politics of Interest Groups
course.description: The course examines the role of interest groups in American politics, particularly how they influence the formulation and implementation of public policy. Specifically, the course focuses on strategies and tactics and other integrated requisites to building a viable interest group. In addition, numerous case studies are examined.

course.title: American Jews/Liberal Democracy
course.description: American Jews have long advanced liberal ideals such as freedom and equality, and they have in turn flourished in a nation that has prized them. However, a liberal society may also be a threat to American Jews. Liberalism, some say, weakens Jewish identity by dissolving religious communities and ties to Israel. This course will explore the complicated relationship between Jews and American liberalism and in so doing draw broader lessons about the liberal dilemmas other ethnic groups face as they seek prosperity and community in America.

course.title: Advanced Conversation through Fi
course.description: This course emphasizes the practice and development of oral communication skills, providing students with the opportunity to engage in the analysis of various social, cultural, and political topics of current interest in Span and Latin America.

course.title: Advanced Conversation through Fi
course.description: This course emphasizes the practice and development of oral communication skills, providing students with the opportunity to engage in the analysis of various social, cultural, and political topics of current interest in Span and Latin America.

course.title: Spanish in the Community
course.description: This course focuses on children of immigration. It explores the forces that shape their adaptation to a new country, their schooling and literacy process, their language use and sense of identity, the relation with family and the cultural processes that take place as they learn to become part of the new society. Readings from social science, literature, and contemporary discussions. Required weekly community service. Prerequisite: Spanish 44 or equivalent.

course.title: Bilingual Lives Belonging & Comm
course.description:
Bilingual Lives: Belonging and Community: This course explores the local and global diverse experiences of bilingual individuals, focusing on how language shapes identity, literacy, and social participation. Students will engage with key sociolinguistic theories and concepts such as bilingualism, language shift, and heritage language maintenance. A central component of the course is community engagement: students will design educational activities and assignments for emergent bilingual students in local schools and implement them in collaboration with classroom teachers to support bilingual literacy.
In addition, students will interview peers from Brazil through a virtual partnership and collaboratively reflect on the meanings of bilingualism, the teaching of foreign languages in middle and high school, and the requirement to demonstrate knowledge of a foreign language for access to higher education. In Brazil, access to foreign language education is often limited by economic factors, creating disparities between students from wealthier backgrounds and those from less privileged contexts. As a result, performance in the foreign language section of the ENEM (Exame Nacional do Ensino Médio) reflects not only linguistic ability but also broader issues of educational inequality and unequal access to opportunities. Through these experiences, students will connect theory, research, and practice, gaining a deeper understanding of bilingualism across diverse sociocultural and educational contexts.

course.title: Strategies of Resistance in Lat
course.description:
This course will examine different recent strategies of political, social, and cultural resistance in Latin American countries, from the cycle of mobilization against neoliberal policies and their effects in the 1990s and 2000s, to the new resistances against ineffectual systems of democratic representation. We will explore cases such as student protests in Chile and Mexico, womens movements in Argentina and Mexico (#NiUnaMenos, #NiUnaMas), as well as some of the contemporary tools of activism and resistance provided by the new global communication networks.
The class will include sources drawn from social sciences, journalism, testimony, film, and literature, and will have a Seminar format.

course.title: Afrolatinidades
course.description: This course examines the black experience in Latin American history and society from the slavery era to present day. Latin America as a vast geographical space cannot possibly be comprehended in one class; therefore, excerpts from a variety of disciplines will be studied thematically in an effort to encompass a broad, but not diluted, understanding of the issues that have historically faced Afro-descendants in the Latin American continent. It will look specifically at the ways in which Afro-Latino artists have represented blackness and designed their own subjectivities and agencies.

course.title: Senior Research Project Seminar
course.description:
This course can take the form of a thesis,
a major essay paper, or another form of applied research. Students will present a
proposal to the faculty at the end of the previous semester. For community-based
research projects students need previous knowledge and collaboration agreements
with the community in question.

course.title: The New Cold War
course.description: Three decades after the end of the Cold War, a new cold war with opposing blocs threatens to plunge the world into a more dangerous era. Economic fragmentation, proxy wars, and an arms race are in full progress even as humanity confronts the existential calamity of climate change. This course examines the origins of the New Cold War, its underlying security and geo-economic drivers, the scope and characteristics of this conflict, the strategies of its primary belligerents and the likely consequences of this conflict.

course.title: Development in Practice
course.description:
"Development" is one of the great intellectual, political, financial, and operational endeavors of our modern global world, and tens of millions of people are active in it, whether as volunteers or as professionals, donors or beneficiaries. This course analyzes the conceptual, policy, and operational debates in the field of international development. The readings come primarily from political science, but also include anthropology and institutional economics. Using these insights, we will analyze the aims, tools, and concrete, day-to-day practices of the people who ?do? development.

Pre-requisite: GOVT 020 CM

course.title: Foreign Relations of the U.S.
course.description: This course will provide insights into the processes and dynamics of US foreign policy, with an emphasis on the complexities of foreign policy-making and contemporary foreign policy issues. The course introduces many of the ideas underpinning American foreign policy and examines how governmental and non-governmental actors drive the country's agenda and its implementation. Students will become familiar with key debates about the US national interest, global challenges, US foreign policy goals, and the means by which they might be achieved.

course.title: The American Founding
course.description: An inquiry into the character of the American regime as intended by the Founders. The method of the course will be the close reading of the writings and speeches of the Founders, supplemented occasionally by secondary accounts and interpretations.

course.title: Intro to Political Philosophy
course.description: An introduction to several fundamentally different philosophical understandings of political life, both ancient and modern. Authors studied include Plato, Aristotle, Aquinas, Machiavelli, Hobbes, Locke, and Rousseau. First semester.

course.title: Topics in Political Philosophy
course.description:
A topic of enquiry will be chosen each semester to reflect current challenges and concerns in the field of political philosophy. 

The topic for Spring 2027 is "Rome and Its Significance for Political Philosophy":

Rome began as a kingdom that was overthrown by a republic, which eventually succumbed to a vast empire.  It was unclear whether the phenomenon of Rome marked the fulfillment of the ancient city?s dreams or the advent of its worst nightmare.  We will study four great interpreters of Rome:  Cicero, Augustine, Machiavelli, and Shakespeare.

course.title: Blackness and the Art of Ocean M
course.description: Blending art, history and science, including oceanography and geology as they intersect with colonial power. Centered on the ocean as a container of memory. Focus on Black lives lost to the ocean during slave trade, and how this loss results in a cultural imprint expressed in contemporary art, including John Akomfrah, Ellen Gallagher, Lorna Simpson, and Jason DeCaires Taylor, and others. Also examines the concept of residence time, a scientific term that refers to how long it takes for the ocean to completely consume something, along with the discovery of the slave ship Clotilda in Alabamaâ¬"s Mobile River Delta.

course.title: Adv Topics in Environ. Science
course.description: Readings and discussion of primary scientific publications on recent environmental science research.  Students also will practice writing for both general and professional scientist audiences, including completion of a review paper.  Topics vary with each offering. Prerequisites: any two from BIOL044L KS, CHEM014L KS, EA  030L KS, EA  055L KS, GEOL020L PO.

course.title: Glaciology with Lab
course.description: Glaciers and ice sheets are Earth's largest stores of freshwater and influence water resources and global sea level. This course examines the physical processes governing glaciers, from the transformation of snow into ice to glacier flow and mass change. Students develop a quantitative understanding of glacier behavior and apply it to mountain glaciers, Greenland, and Antarctica. Computational labs use Python and QGIS to analyze glaciological data and investigate glacier and ice sheet processes.

course.title: Glaciology
course.description: Glaciers and ice sheets are Earth's largest stores of freshwater and influence water resources and global sea level. This course examines the physical processes governing glaciers, from the transformation of snow into ice to glacier flow and mass change. Students develop a quantitative understanding of glacier behavior and apply it to analyses of mountain glaciers, Greenland, and Antarctica. Prerequisite: one intro lab course from among EA 030L KS, EA 055L KS, GEOL020L PO.

course.title: Imaging Tools for Biol. Sys.
course.description: This half-course explores how light-emitting tools are used to study biological processes, ranging from gene expression to interactions between biomolecules to cancer metathesis. This course will focus on the chemical theory behind how light is produced, as well as foundational and recent literature related to how these chemical tools have been used to answer biological questions.

course.title: Adv. Lab in Neuroscience
course.description: An advanced laboratory course centered on a semester-long research investigation in neuroscience. Students develop hypotheses, design, conduct experiments, and analyze original data to explore phenomenon in neuroscience. Topics, experimental systems, and methods vary by semester. Emphasis is placed on authentic research, experimental design, quantitative analysis, scientific literature, and scientific communication. Prerequisites: BIOL043L KS and CHEM014LKS, or CHEM029L KS. NEUR095L JT strongly recommended.

course.title: Immunology w/Lab
course.description: The vertebrate immune system is a complex network of organs, cells, molecules, and pathways that recognizes and destroys pathogens and responds to diverse antigens, from microbial surface tags to synthetic structures. This course surveys the molecular, cellular, and genetic basis of immunity in humans. We will also investigate the molecular and cellular basis of immunodeficiencies, autoimmune disorders, and other diseases to understand what happens when immunity fails or becomes overactive.

course.title: Security Studies
course.description: This course will introduce students to the study of how states provide for their security through the use of military force. The course will first explore the origin and nature of threats to states' security. It will then examine the key military implements and strategies that states employ in attempting to deal with these threats. Finally the course will study several historical cases of military conflict in light of its earlier theoretical and strategic findings.

course.title: War II: Film
course.description: Innumerable excellent films have used depictions of war to examine politics, power dynamics, international relations, institutions, ethics, history, social evolution, leadership, identity, community, and human nature. This seminar course will rely on a combination of films, readings, and research to deeply examine these issues in light of contemporary international security. This course serves as a complement and supplement to War, but stands independently. Prerequisite - GOVT020  CM.

course.title: Special Topics in Intl Relations
course.description:
Special Topics in International Relations. Topics vary from semester to semester. 
In this research seminar, students will do in-depth research on alternative conceptions and concrete initiatives that seek to advance very different visions of development. Who is out there thinking of radically different ways of defining the good society and the good life? What are they proposing to do to make it happen? How would we judge these alternatives, and what are their costs? Pre-requisite: GOVT020 CM

The topic for Fall 2026 is: "Alternatives to Development"
Development is one of the great intellectual, political, and financial endeavors of our modern world. It is the dominant global vision of the good society, of greatly enhanced consumption and freedom for all individuals?so everyone can live like how the world thinks Americans live. Today, many people are not so sure anymore that development is a dream and not a nightmare. They wonder about its costs, about what is being lost, about the risks ahead. They are searching not for alternatives ways of doing development, but for actual alternatives to development.

course.title: Reading for Pleasure, Age of AI
Developmental Cell Biology
course.description: The development of an embryo from a single cell to a complex body requires the coordinated efforts of a growing number of cells and cell types. In this course, students will learn the fundamental cell biological and genetic mechanisms that make development possible, including intercellular signaling, gene expression regulation, cell migration, differentiation, and morphogenesis. Central to this course is a focus on modern techniques for interrogating developmental questions such as stem cell models, advanced microscopy, synthetic biology, and genomics. Students will also learn how developmental processes, when disrupted, lead to cancer and other diseases.

course.title: Sem: Meditation/Mindfulness
course.description: The practice of meditation and mindfulness is deeply rooted in many Eastern healing traditions. Mindfulness and meditation have been shown to be beneficial for reducing stress, improving mental and physical well-being, and increasing focus and performance outcomes. In addition, the practice of mindfulness has been integrated into Western psychotherapy and evidence-based practices. This course is designed to provide a multifaceted understanding of mindfulness and meditation. We will examine historical and contemporary issues, review and practice different types of mindfulness, examine the physiological underpinnings of mindfulness, and research how mindfulness can be beneficial across a variety of domains. Prerequisite - one previous course in psychology

course.title: Codes
course.description: Students will learn foundational principles in the sciences, experimental methods, as well as data science and computer science concepts for scientific insight, including Python programming. No prior science or computing experience is expected.

course.title: Public Health Praxis
course.description: This course takes a multi-disciplinary approach to examine educational and professional pathways as a sociopolitical determinant of racial health equity. The course introduces students to theoretical frameworks, extant public health research, and community-driven actions that challenge conventional approaches to public health in the United States. By interrogating historical and contemporary conditions affecting people with Asian and Pasifika ancestry, students will critique academic, labor, and health care structures that maintain barriers to collective liberation. Students will explore diverse pathways to working toward healthy futures for all by centering the perspectives of community organizers, scholar-activists, artists, and health professionals serving Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander communities.

course.title: Central American Cinema
course.description:
"This course explores Central American cinema with a focused emphasis on gender representation and migration narratives. Through films from Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, and Panama, students will examine how filmmakers depict identity, displacement, borders, labor, family, and power. Special attention is given to womenâ¬"s experiences, masculinity, queer identities, and the socio-political realities of migration within and beyond the region.

Learning Objectives
By the end of the course, students will be able to:
- Analyze representations of gender and migration in film
- Understand the historical and political contexts shaping Central American cinema
- Evaluate how cinema constructs narratives of identity, displacement, and belonging
- Apply film theory (feminist, postcolonial, transnational) to film analysis - Produce critical written and oral arguments"

course.title: Mapping Latinx Identies
course.description: This course interrogates the theoretical and material construction of the Nuevo South," with an analytical focus on the Mississippi socio-political and geographic landscape. By deconstructing the regionâ¬"s traditional Black-White racial binary, we examine how the stateâ¬"s legacies of Jim Crow and industrial agriculturalâ¬specifically the poultry, cotton, and tobacco industriesâ¬have mediated the incorporation and racialization of Latinx migrants. Through a multi-scalar lens, students will investigate the historical presence of Mexicanos in the Delta, the contemporary flows of Central American labor into the "Poultry Belt," and the Afro-Latinx (Garifuna) maritime networks of the Gulf Coast. Ultimately, the course asks how migration challenges and reinforces the "Deep South" as a site of both racial exclusion and transnational possibility.

course.title: Intro: Design Applied Sciences
course.description:
How do we turn an idea into a practical solution to a real-world problem? This course introduces students to the process of design: identifying a problem, understanding the needs of the people affected by it, developing possible solutions, building and testing prototypes, and improving those solutions based on evidence and feedback. Working in small teams, students will tackle open-ended problems, learning how to balance competing goals, practical constraints, and the needs of potential users. Through hands-on projects, students will develop skills in creative problem-solving, experimentation, teamwork, and communication. No prior engineering or design experience is required. Not open to students who have completed ENGR004 HM. 
Prerequisite: SCI 010L CM or permission of instructor.

course.title: Mathematical Modeling for Scient
course.description: This course provides a broad introduction to mathematical modeling as it applies to the life and Earth sciences. It covers both analytic and computational techniques used to generate model predictions about the natural world and includes detailed case studies of models commonly used in a variety of scientific disciplines, such as biochemistry, ecology, epidemiology, and climate science. Prerequisites: SCI 050L CM, or permission of the instructor.

course.title: Biochemistry
course.description: This course combines principles from organic chemistry, molecular biology, and physical chemistry to explore the molecular structures and chemical processes necessary for life. The structure and function of biomolecules will be applied to enzyme kinetics and catalysis, metabolic pathways, broader bioenergetics concepts, and regulation. The laboratory will provide experience with isolating and characterizing biological molecules in the context of discovery-based projects.   Prerequisites: SCI 031LA CM, SCI 031LB CM, and SCI 111L  CM.

course.title: Medical Microbiology & Infection
course.description: This course provides an overview of basic principles in infectious disease caused by major microbial pathogens. Through lectures and discussion of assigned reading material, the course examines current and classical topics in the field of host-pathogen relationships with an emphasis on the interplay between pathogen strategies and the host response. Students will be expected to give oral presentations on review of primary literature in infectious disease and participate in regular class discussions of research papers. Prerequisites: SCI 031LA CM and SCI 031LB CM. Course is equivalent to BIOL168L KS and BIOL189L PO.

course.title: Fields and Waves
course.description: This course expands on the fundamental principles of physics and how they are integral to the themes of health, brain, and planet. Topics include static and moving charges, electromagnetism, wave phenomena, and a practical introduction to quantum mechanics and nuclear physics. The lab portion of this course focuses on experimental design, data collection, and statistical data analysis, including the quantification of uncertainties. Prerequisites: SCI 030LACM, SCI 030LBCM, and MATH031 (or higher).

course.title: Fields and Waves
course.description: This course expands on the fundamental principles of physics and how they are integral to the themes of health, brain, and planet. Topics include static and moving charges, electromagnetism, wave phenomena, and a practical introduction to quantum mechanics and nuclear physics. The lab portion of this course focuses on experimental design, data collection, and statistical data analysis, including the quantification of uncertainties. Prerequisites: SCI 030LACM, SCI 030LBCM, and MATH031 (or higher).

course.title: Golf
course.description:
This class is open to golfers of all levels.  Golfers will receive instruction suited to their level of experience and skill in the game.

The course will cover putting, chipping, pitch shots, full-swing mechanical instruction, golf etiquette, and rules instruction.  It will utilize the golf practice center immediately to the north of the Axelrood Swimming Pool at Claremont McKenna.

If students have their own clubs, they should bring them to class.  If not, clubs will be provided.

course.title: Golf
course.description:
This class is open to golfers of all levels.  Golfers will receive instruction suited to their level of experience and skill in the game.

The course will cover putting, chipping, pitch shots, full-swing mechanical instruction, golf etiquette, and rules instruction.  It will utilize the golf practice center immediately to the north of the Axelrood Swimming Pool at Claremont McKenna.

If students have their own clubs, they should bring them to class.  If not, clubs will be provided.

course.title: Introduction to Political Studie
course.description: What is the relationship between politics and political science?  This course introduces the study of modern politics. The first half of the class examines the creation of modern politics and its study before academic political science emerged; the second half of the class examines its study since the founding of the discipline. Topics include problems of rule, revolutionary political action, the pivotal role of the Progressives, the contested globalization of American forms of political science, and the shuddering foundations of the study of politics today. [Note: This is one of the introductory courses for the Pitzer Political Studies major.]

course.title: Sounds & Sonics of Black Life
course.description: This course will help students consider how we listen to, create, and critique a multitude of Black musical styles and genres - from the soulful stylings of Aretha Franklin and Celia Cruz to the contemporary experimentation and innovation of Tierra Whack and Kendrick Lamar - in conversation with writers like Zora Neale Hurston, Kofi Agawu, Sylvia Wynter, Katherine McKittrick, and Maureen Mahon who help us better understand the sound and significance of their performances. Students will be expected to engage the dynamic rhythms and melodies of Black social life by sharpening their critical listening practice and thoughtfully engaging in cultural critique. In doing so students will broaden their musical and cultural horizons and situate Black diasporic music making in the 20th and 21st centuries within a broader context of racial capitalism, commodification, global networks of exchange, and the artistic pathways forged from legacies of joy, sorrow, pleasure, and struggle.

course.title: Islamic Art and Architecture
course.description: An introduction to the art and architecture of the Islamic lands, beginning with the early years of Islam and moving chronologically to the contemporary period. The course focuses on key objects and monuments from regions including Islamic Spain, North Africa, the eastern Mediterranean, Iran, Central Asia, and South Asia. Examines a range of examples to discuss interpretive issues related to production, reception, and meaning. Explores the history of Islamic art and also considers contemporary global issues from an art historical perspective.

course.title: Hip Hop Music Video & Film
course.description:
Course examines Hip Hop music video and film as dynamic sites of visual, sonic, and lyrical aesthetics through Kendrick Lamar and co-director Dave Free (The Little Homies), in collaboration with choreographer Charm La'Donna's manipulation of space and movement as expressive beats, bars, and flow.

Course focuses on formal analysis of Lamar's six albums and music videos (2011-2025) and his Super Bowl Halftime Show, exploring intertextuality, sampling, and visual storytelling. Students analyze iconography, symbolism, poetic metaphor, sonic texture, and elements of mise-en-scène, and rhythmic editing across music videos, short and feature-length films, and live performance.

Historical context traces Hip Hop sampling from blues, jazz, funk, soul, and R&B, examining the genre's transformation of the 9 Elements and 4 Principles. Drawing on perspectives from video essayists, journalists, podcasters, and rappers, students study Hip Hop Kulture in dialogue with art, cinema, and global media.

course.title: Sculpture 1 - The Reductive
course.description: As a foundational method within sculpture, Carving and Shaping Realities focuses on the reductive processes employed by carving, scraping, rasping, and sanding.  Students will engage a wide variety of tools and make some of their own given the unique needs their ideas demand.  Expect to engage a wide variety of materials - foam, plaster, wood, and stone. Letter grade only.

course.title: Weaving as Art: Tapestry & Loom
course.description:
This is a studio art course on the art of weaving in a contemporary context.  The two primary forms of weaving, small frame tapestry and floor loom weaving will be the methods of production.

Course content will cover materials, yarn and thread, the tools and techniques involved with the looms and the making of image and pattern.  Process and concept will lead the way in artistic exploration as the materials take form. 

The global history of fiber and textiles and the work of contemporary artists will inform our making. 

Visiting artists, readings and films will add to our knowledge of creative exploration in a socio-historical context.

course.title: Rethinking Painting
course.description:
Painting carries the weight of an enormous history and an intricate and involved technical language. Yet, despite its long lineage, painting continues to transform and challenge its boundaries. Why are we still painting? No longer confined to being a decorative object hung on the wall, painting has become a site for artists to interrogate traditions, engage with contemporary issues, and reinvent what a painted surface can mean. This course invites you to rethink painting?not just as a medium, but as an activity, and an evolving language that speaks to not only identity and culture, but the limits of representation itself.

We will focus on developing a rigorous studio practice with painting: exploration of ideas, styles, and creative expression related to more complex subject matter and concepts using a variety of mediums, techniques, and methodologies together with critical discussions on current issues in painting. Prerequisites: Art 110

course.title: General Chemistry w/Laboratory
course.description: General Chemistry with Lab. An introduction to the theories exploring the physical and chemical properties of the elements and their compounds, including the structure and properties of solids, liquids and gases. Topics include nuclear chemistry, quantum theory, atomic and molecular structure via orbital theory, chemical bonding, coordination chemistry, spectroscopy, chemical kinetics and the properties of multicomponent solutions and electrolytes. Laboratory work is coordinated with the lecture and emphasizes quantitative analytical and instrumental techniques. Pre-requisite: CHEM 010A PO.

Laboratory work is coordinated with the lecture and emphasizes quantitative analytical and instrumental techniques. Pre-requisite: CHEM 010A PO.

course.title: Discovering Chemistry w/ Lab
course.description: An introduction to chemistry and chemical discovery using a course-based undergraduate research experience in which the whole class will address research questions with unknown outcomes that are of interest to the broader scientific community. Laboratory work emphasizes experimental planning and practice, chemical synthesis, analytical techniques, and molecular modeling. Lecture is coordinated with the laboratory and further develops concepts of molecular structure, intermolecular forces, acid?base chemistry, equilibria, thermodynamics, chemical kinetics, and molecular recognition.

course.title: Physical Chemistry w/Lab
course.description: Foundational Physical Chemistry provides an integrated introduction to the core theoretical and experimental frameworks that underpin modern chemistry. The course establishes a foundation in quantum mechanics, thermodynamics, and chemical kinetics, offering students a unified perspective on how structure, energy, and dynamics govern molecular systems. Laboratory emphasizes modern instrumental and computational methods and advanced data analysis.

course.title: Enviro Analyt Chem W/Lab
course.description: The course combines traditional quantitative analysis content delivered in context of environmental chemical analyses with an emphasis on laboratory work. It introduces students to the main compartments of the environment, the atmosphere, hydrosphere and lithosphere, and the chemical and physical interactions among them. The laboratory work will be a project-based laboratory focused on porous, crystalline materials (metal organic frameworks) that may be used to improve water quality. Oral presentations and formal laboratory reports required.

course.title: Inorganic Chemistry w/ Lab
course.description: The structure, bonding, and reactivity of inorganic molecules and solids are discussed using a symmetry and molecular orbital based approach. Additional topics including ligand field, hard/soft acid-base theories, as well as physical organometallic chemistry will be discussed with applications in spectroscopy, organometallic catalysis, and bioinorganic chemistry. Prerequisites: Chem 101 PO.

course.title: Biochemistry w/Laboratory
course.description: Biological molecules considered in terms of their structure and roles in the dynamic processes by which energy and information are received, interconverted and transmitted in order to maintain life. Laboratory emphasizes techniques and instrumentation used to study the nature of biochemical molecules and processes.

course.title: NMR Spectroscopy
course.description: Examines fundamental concepts in nuclear magnetic resonance with a focus on spectroscopic techniques used for organic structure elucidation and conformational analysis. Hands-on experience with data collection and analysis. Letter grade only. Prerequisites: CHEM101 PO.

course.title: NMR Spectroscopy
course.description: Examines fundamental concepts in nuclear magnetic resonance with a focus on spectroscopic techniques used for organic structure elucidation and conformational analysis. Hands-on experience with data collection and analysis. Letter grade only. Prerequisites: CHEM101 PO.

course.title: Intro to Medicinal Chemistry
course.description: Medicinal chemistry  explores how chemical principles are applied to the discovery and development of drugs.  Students learn how molecular structure influences biological activity, pharmacokinetics, and drug safety. The course introduces key concepts such as structure?activity relationships, drug targets, and basic metabolism. Emphasis is placed on connecting chemistry to real-world therapeutic applications.  Prerequisite: CHEM 105 PO

course.title: International Interethnic China
course.description: This is a fourth-year Chinese language acquisition course. The class focuses on topics related to international and interethnic exchanges that have taken place in China in the modern era (roughly 19th century-present). Students will learn to approach China from an international and interethnic perspective by tracing key moments in modern China's encounter with both the world outside it and the ethnic minority groups within it. Students will study historical photography, documents, watch movies, and read essays related to how international and interethnic exchanges have shaped China's national identity and cultural identity. Students will both develop their Chinese language skills and gain important insights into China's relationship to the multicultural modern world.

course.title: Archaeology and Society
course.description: Who owns the past? What are the aims of archaeology? How have the motivations and methods of early archaeologists and collectors defined what we know now? Could current projects radically transform our understanding of the ancient world? In this course, we will work together as an intellectual community to deepen our understanding of ethical issues raised by the practices of archaeology, museology, and the collection and display of material culture. We will begin by studying several archaeological projects and artifact collections from the ancient Mediterranean, including Troy, Knossos, the Parthenon Marbles, and the antiquities collection of the J. Paul Getty Museum in Malibu. Students will then identify, research, and present relevant case studies of significant interest to the students themselves. By applying diverse theoretical models, including actor-network modeling, thing theory, decoloniality, and feminism, we will develop our own methodologies for the study of archaeology in social context. Additional course information for fall 2020.

course.title: Algorithmic Game Theory
course.description: Algorithmic Game Theory studies the design and analysis of algorithms in environments with multiple self-interested participants. This interdisciplinary course equips students with the vocabulary and modeling tools needed to reason about such settings. We will study how to design mechanisms that incentivize truthful behavior, how auctions allocate scarce resources, how matching algorithms and voting rules aggregate individual preferences, and how selfish behavior impacts system performance. Through theoretical analysis and case studies, students will learn how algorithmic choices interact with strategic behavior and how this interaction shapes outcomes. No prior background in game theory will be assumed.

course.title: Presentation Performance Lab
course.description: This course is designed to help students become more comfortable speaking and presenting material in front of an audience. Students interested in performing arts,public speaking, academic presentation, and those who wish to become more proficient at job interviews, will explore their own passions and skill sets, as well as investigate areas they find themselves less attuned to. Class time will serve as a laboratory for students to bring in presentation and performance related activities that interest them, including but not limited to acting, music, dance, oral interpretation of literature (recitation of poetry and prose), oral reports, speeches, debate, and public speaking of all kinds.

course.title: The Environmental Polycrisis
course.description:
We live amid social and political upheaval, accelerating climate disruption, and a sixth mass extinction. While turbulence in society is not new, today?s environmental crises are unprecedented and moving past tipping points. Rising authoritarianism blocks efforts to address climate and species loss, strengthening petrochemical and extractive industries. Activists have struggled to create lasting change. Why is that? We all face urgent questions in these times: how do we act with courage and creativity in the pursuit of the goals that matter to us; how do we stay meaningful without guarantees of success in our various aims; how do we care for ourselves as we work to build a better future?

This course invites students to explore both scholarly and experiential approaches, integrating intellectual study with reflective practices to understand our place as embodied beings on Earth.

course.title: Philosophies of Place
course.description: What is the role of place in human life? How has place historically been valued across different philosophical traditions? How does the significance of place point beyond a merely human world? This course examines individual and collective identity in relation to space and place from a philosophical perspective. We analyze the theoretical and practical significance of place through the concepts of home, dwelling, technology, embodiment, environment, power, globalization, and decolonization. Our readings draw from multiple traditions, including Continental philosophy, Indigenous thought, phenomenology, critical geography, prison studies, and the environmental humanities. While we work to develop a philosophical accounting of place, we will also actively cultivate a deeper relationship with Southern California through site-specific readings.

course.title: California Beaches
course.description: This course represents an interdisciplinary exploration of the science, history, and policy challenges of California's beaches and coast. It will explore: the formation and dynamic character of beaches; evolving uses of beaches including recreation and resource extraction; political contests over access and protection; and future policy challenges posed by climate change.

course.title: Applied Econometrics
course.description: This course teaches quantitative methods for testing economic models, with a focus on linear regression analysis and casual inference. The key focus is the design and implementation of an empirical research paper. The course develops the student's understanding and analysis of data through frequent empirical assignments. Prerequisites: ECON 051 PO or ECON 101 PO; ECON 052 PO or ECON 102 PO; ECON 057 PO.

course.title: Economics of Financial Markets
course.description: This course provides an introduction to finance and the economic roles played by financial markets. Finance topics include asset pricing, capital budgeting, risk management, options and derivatives. Economic issues include the informational efficiency of financial markets; the impact of markets for time, risk and optionality on economic outcomes and risk; and policy responses to potential sources of economic inefficiency or fragility. While not a course on asset management, it will examine how developments in finance are impacting this industry.

course.title: Economics of Gender & the Family
course.description: The Economics of Gender and the Family. Analysis of the factors contributing to the economic circumstances of women and men in modern market economies, especially the United States. Trends in labor-force participation, occupational choice and the economic determinants of earnings, household income and poverty. Prerequisites: 52 or 102.

course.title: Senior Seminar in Economics
course.description: Analysis of selected problems in economics. Required for graduation. Full course credit. Prerequisites: ECON 101 PO, ECON 102 PO and either ECON 107 PO or ECON 167 PO must be completed in advance of participating in the Senior Seminar.

course.title: Poetry Starting with Words
course.description: A poem is a list of words, but it isn't only words. Although "it is true that many poems are constructed solely of words," according to the poet Barbara Guest, "we have all read these poems and we know that after we have read them we feel curiously bereft." This introductory course studies poems as words on a page, as sounds, as images, as ideas, and as artifacts. Examples from poems by Milton, Marvell, Pope, Burns, and Dickinson, as well as some anonymous ballads and riddles.

course.title: Group Texts: Genres of U.S. Lit
course.description: This class will offer an introduction to key terms and texts in U.S. literature in order to provide a grounding for more advanced study in a national literary tradition. Students should leave this class with a knowledge of many foundational texts in the field, as well as an understanding of the evolution of genre within the field. Key terms will include gender and genre, aesthetics and politics, race and freedom, domesticity and empire, nation and hemisphere, art, democracy and representation.

course.title: The Poetic Sequence
course.description: In this workshop, students will produce a chapbook-length series of poems concerning a central theme or formal constraint. Students will focus on research methods for creative writing and develop strategies to sustain a writing practice. We will consider how poems are in conversation with each other, as well as identify and build a vocabulary for the aesthetic qualities that make a writer unique. We will analyze and discuss the works of established literary figures such as Walt Whitman, Muriel Rukeyser, John Berryman, Rita Dove, Louise Gluck, Natasha Trethewey, Victoria Chang, Terrance Hayes, Patricia Smith, Diane Seuss, Tyehimba Jess, Gabrielle Calvocoressi, Maggie Nelson, Ross Gay, and Paisley Rekdal.

course.title: Continuing Introductory French
course.description: Introductory French. Development of speaking, listening, reading and writing skills. Intensive conversation and oral and written exercises. Pictures, videos, films, stories and realia from Francophone culture. Increased emphasis on reading and writing skills in second semester. Prerequisites: FREN001 PO. Course is equivalent to FREN002  CM, FREN002  PZ, and FREN002  SC.

course.title: Art, Politics & Power in France
course.description:
This course explores the complex relationships between art, politics, and power in France from the Ancien Régime to the present day. Through the lens of famous art thefts (from the Mona Lisa to the Crown Jewels) and literary figures such as Arsène Lupin, we will examine how works of art have become instruments of power, national symbols, and major economic stakes.

The course alternates between historical narrative (the creation of museums, the birth of cultural heritage, cultural policies) and thematic reflections (patronage, the art market, restitution), punctuated by criminal investigations that reveal the passions these objects inspire.

course.title: Oceans and Climate
course.description: This course covers basic principles of chemical and physical oceanography and the interplay between the oceans and planetary climate. Topics include: origin of oceans, ocean circulation, marine biogeochemical cycles and the interplay between oceans and climate. Emphasis on specific topics is subject to change from year to year depending on student interests. A quantitative component introduces students to simple geochemical modeling (e.g. box models of element cycling). A blend of lectures, student-led seminar discussions, and hands-on modeling exercises will make up class meetings. Prerequisites: either GEOL 015 PO or any version of GEOL020 or EA 100L KS or an introductory level chemistry course CHEM 001A, CHEM 023A or CHEM 051, or introductory physics course PHYS 041 or PHYS 042. The course is offered as an intermediate level elective.

course.title: Deutschland in Schwarz und Weiss
course.description: Based on a blend of texts, this cultural-studies course provides a survey of the current state of race relations and racial discourse in the German-speaking countries. It draws on input from literary sources, discussions in media, presentations in film and other visuals, and experiences in daily life. The course will also facilitate conversations on (colonial) history, comparison of racial issues and racism between the Germanic countries and the USA, and provide broader context for aspects of (labor) migration, refugee policies, and the persistence of xenophobia and right-wing ideologies. The course will also present national and transnational efforts (for instance via the EU) to address the social ills of racism and discrimination. Prerequisites: GERM044  PO.

course.title: Germany Black and White
course.description: This is a half-credit English-language version of the German-language GERM180  PO offered for all students who do not have advanced German language capabilities (German-44 or higher to enroll in the full credit GERM180  PO) but are interested in the thematics. Based on a blend of sources, this cultural-studies course provides a survey of the current state of race relations and racial discourse in the German-speaking countries. It draws on input from literary texts, discussions in media, presentations in film and other visuals, and experiences in daily life. A key goal of the course is, beyond the broad content focus on questions of race, migration, xenophobia, class, and DEI, to offer an alternative view of these topics beyond the US-American debate. Many students are doubtlessly already acquainted with the latter, and the course provides a new lens on these questions through the cultural historical parameters of a different country/culture. Lastly, the course also presents national and transnational efforts (for instance via the EU) to address the social ills of racism and discrimination.

course.title: Age of Conquest and Continuity
course.description: A writing intensive examination of the collision of worlds that began in 1492, primarily focusing on the sixteenth century.  This period has become known as the Spanish Conquest of the Americas.  A master narrative passed down by generations of historians tells a near mythical narrative of Europeans, technologies, and disease swiftly overwhelming Indigenous societies.  Students will explore primary and secondary sources to examine to what extent that actually occurred.  By focusing on people from Indigenous America, Europe, and Africa who experienced the upheavals of the sixteenth century, this class presents a new conquest history, one that finds continuity as the period?s principal feature.  The conquest was not a short event, but a slow process marked by violence, but also new global relationships.  Over the course of the class, students will also compose a research paper based on original primary source research.

course.title: The Chinese Diaspora
course.description: Examines the history of Chinese emigration in the 20th century, its political and social implications to China, its peripheries and the rest of the world. Topics will include the concept of "diaspora," "Sinophone" studies, the sense of belonging among overseas Chinese, community and identity formations. Letter grade only. (Asia) Previously offered as HIST100CDPO.

course.title: Citizen Participation in Lat Am
course.description: In this class, students will learn about the institutional innovations public officials and historically marginalized groups (women, people of color, members of the LGBTQ+ community, migrants and their descendants, low-income groups, and others) have come up with in order to make public policies more inclusive around the world. A particular emphasis will be given to Latin America and other regions from the Global South, where most of these innovations are being created. Although Participatory Budgeting (PB) is the most famous of these innovations, the class will critically examine PB and many others as well as the multiple ways in which they have become globalized as different actors share them and/or transform them into international best practices. Letter grade only. Previously offered as SOC 189K PO.

course.title: Capitalism, Technology & Race
course.description: This course places the concept of "race" as central to critical media as well as science and technology studies. We will study how historians and theorists have discussed the concept as part of the rise of modern capitalist society. We will look at the role of technology as a material force that delineates the parameters of profit accumulation, exploitation, and social distinction in order to better conceptualize the notions of race in our contemporary digital society.

course.title: Group Guitar
course.description: Students will be introduced to the fundamentals of classical guitar technique and repertoire, developing musicianship skills through engagement with notated music and chord charts. No experience is required, but students must have a nylon-string classical guitar (can be borrowed through the Music Department) and guitar footstool. Priority for private lessons in guitar will be given to students who have taken this course.

course.title: Music in Punjabi Culture
course.description: Examination of musical life in Punjab (India-Pakistan cross-border region) and the Punjabi Diaspora, with emphasis on the changing role of music and dance in new social contexts. Analyzes how music is mapped upon such social dimensions as gender, class, and ethnicity, and the impact of media, emigration, and globalization.

course.title: Musical Mathematics
course.description: This course examines mathematical approaches to understanding music as well as musical repertoire that has a basis in mathematical principles. Considers the philosophical foundations for the study of musical proportion, and explores topics including musical set theory, group theory, graph theory, and geometries of music. Analyzes examples of Baroque counterpoint, 19th-century chromatic music, 20th-century concert music, world music, and American popular music. Some prior knowledge of either music or mathematics is helpful but not necessary. Letter grade only.

course.title: The Rhythmic Brain w/Lab
course.description: This course explores how organisms from bacteria to humans measure and anticipate time. We will examine how the molecular gears of the circadian clock generate daily rhythms in physiology and behavior, how internal rhythms are set and reset by environmental cues such as light and temperature, and what happens when these rhythms are disrupted (e.g., jet lag, shift work). We will also cover rhythms beyond the 24-hour cycle, including pulsatile hormone release, tidal rhythms in behavior, and seasonal timing.

course.title: Body&Strength Interval Training
course.description: Class focus: Strength training that will utilize your own body weight while also incorporating weights. Workouts are high intensity and will mix cardiovascular development and overall strength building. Exercises are timed and done in a group setting. P/NP grading only. May be repeated 8 times for credit. Additional course information for fall 2020.

locations: Ctr for Ath, Rec & Well STU1

course.title: Pilates-Yoga Blend
course.description: This class explores the foundational Yoga Asanas (postures) and provides students with a solid understanding of the Traditional Pilates Matwork exercises. By blending these two disciplines, students learn how they are similar as well as how they differ. Through this contrast, a deeper understanding of each is acquired. Students will cultivate strength/stability within the body while learning to allow for equal flexibly and range of motion in the process. P/NP grading only. Course may be repeated 8 times for credit. Additional course information for fall 2020.

locations: Ctr for Ath, Rec & Well STU2

course.title: Care & Prev of Athletic Injuries
course.description: Theory and practice in the care and prevention of injuries commonly encountered in athletics and physical education. Lecture, lab and demonstration. Does not satisfy the Physical Education requirement.

course.title: Advanced Logic
course.description: This course has two main parts. 1. Metalogic: Can we prove that standard logic is consistent? Are all logical truths provable? We will give precise content to these questions and answer them. We will consider implications for the foundations of mathematics, the original context in which metalogical questions were raised, as well as the role of metalogic for the foundations of computer science. 2. Modal logic: modal logic is the logic of what is necessary and possible. We will study standard systems of modal logic and important applications for formalizing reasoning that are not well captured by mathematical logic. Overall, this course will provide an understanding of the point of formal logic and will also help students understand the crucial role formal logic has played in the development of contemporary philosophy and associated fields such as mathematics and computer science.

course.title: Introductory Classical Mechanics
course.description: Introductory Classical Mechanics.  An introduction to classical mechanics, emphasizing the centrality of the fundamental conservation laws of Newtonian mechanics and focusing on applying Newtons Laws of Motion and their consequences to standard physical systems such as the simple harmonic oscillator and planetary motion. Prerequisites: PHYS 70 and completion of/or concurrent enrollment in MATH 30. First years only; others only with permission. Half course.

course.title: Experimental Optics
course.description: A hands-on introduction to optical instruments and techniques. Ray optics, building simple instruments, light detection methods, interference, and diffraction will be covered in this studio course that blends lectures, problem solving, and lab activities. Prerequisites: PHYS070  PO or MATH030  PO. Co-requisites: PHYS101  PO.

course.title: Modern Political Theory
course.description: Modern Political Theory. Second half of sequence, but does not require or presuppose 1A (Classical Political Theory). Themes and concepts associated with modernity: social-contract theory; equality and rights; the origins of democracy, liberalism and individualism; the origins of protest, revolution and radicalism; and economics and the bureaucratic state.

course.title: Green Political Theory
course.description: Green Political Theory: Ecology, Environmentalism, and Apocalypse. Readings include works from George Kateb, Leslie Paul Thiele, Wendell Berry, bell hooks, Tim Mulgan, Heidegger, Spinoza, Emerson and others. Prerequisite: at least one course in political theory.

course.title: Law and Politics
course.description: Law and Politics. This course examines the intersection of law, politics, and policy in the American context.  It investigates the opportunities and pitfalls of legal advocacy, the relationship between litigation and legislation and the nature of judicial interpretation and policy-making.  In doing so, it explores the ways in which legal decisions and processes shape and are shaped by political and institutional conditions. Prerequisites: POLI003  PO.

course.title: Human Neuroscience
course.description: Introduction to the relationship between the human nervous system and mental processes and behavior. Fundamentals of the structure and function of the human nervous system will be introduced, and its relationship to sensation, perception, motivation, emotion, cognition, social interaction and pathological behavior will be explored. Lecture and discussion. Letter grade only. Prerequisite: PSYC051  PO.

course.title: Psych of the Black Experience
course.description: Psychology of the Black Experience. Facilitates students understanding of the African-American psychological experience. Critical review of historical and traditional approaches to the psychological study of Black people; examines  the contributions of the first three generations of Black psychologists who set the foundations for the current generation. Concludes with a look at Black psychology today and its influence on the mainstream of the field. Prerequisite: 51.

course.title: Emotion & Motivation with Lab
course.description: Emotions permeate our lives and guide human behavior. In this course, we will cover the major theories and findings in the scientific study of emotions and motivation. In addition, the lab component of this course will emphasize methodological training in how to measure and manipulate emotions, culminating in a research and analysis project of student-collected data.

course.title: Seminar in Clinical Psychology
course.description: Focuses on fundamental issues related to the practice and research of adult psychotherapy from theoretical, empirical, and applied perspectives. Includes discussion of issues and controversies related to the history of psychotherapy, psychotherapy research, and contemporary psychotherapy practice.  Emphasizes critical thinking, discussion, and writing. Letter grade only. Prerequisite: PSYC 131  PO.

course.title: Latinx Mental Health
course.description: This seminar will explore current issues related to Latinx Mental Health. Using a culturally-informed, bio-psycho-social framework, this course will expose students to the risk and protective factors that impact the etiology, development, and treatments of psychological disorders and related conditions among Latinx populations in the United States. Students are expected to contribute to a class project focused on identifying and addressing a gap in culturally-informed mental health resources and services among the greater Los Angeles area Latinx communities. Letter grade only. Prerequisites: PSYC131  PO or PSYC084  CH.

course.title: Jewish Mysticism
course.description: Jewish Mysticism. Close reading of selections from various texts of medieval Jewish mysticism in translation, including the Zohar, Abulafia, Cordovero, Luria and the Hasidim.

course.title: Senior Thesis
course.description: Senior Thesis. Required of all senior majors in religious studies.

course.title: Readings in Modern Russian Lit
course.description: A survey of Russian and Soviet poetry, prose and film of the 20th century, covering major cultural movements including symbolism, futurism, ornamental prose, socialist realism, literature of the thaw, dissident and underground culture and the post-Soviet scene. Class discussion in both Russian and English. Focus on composition in Russian. Prerequisite: RUSS044  PO

course.title: Introduction to Sociology
course.description: Introduction to Sociology. Characteristics of groups, institutions, society and culture. Social interaction, self-image, status. Brief consideration of social change, ethnicity, the urban environment and demography. Course is equivalent to SOC 001  PZ.

course.title: Media and Society
course.description: This course applies the insights of sociology to the study of media and culture. It examines the role media play in various social phenomena, including interaction, power, and identity. It combines this sociological perspective with a historical one, exploring in turn the sociological dimensions of print, electronic, and digital media. Students will be encouraged to reflexively consider the role of media in their own lives. Letter grade only.

course.title: Gender and Embodiment
course.description: Explores the cultural and political dimensions of gender,the body and society. Topics include a discussion of cosmetic surgery, modeling and the veil. We will consider gendered bodies within the context of institutions such as the media, medicine and the market. Letter grade only.

course.title: Intro to Literary Analysis
course.description: Introduction to Literary Analysis. Analysis of literary genres and styles. Introduction to methods of literary criticism; practice in interpretation of texts. Required of majors. Prerequisite: 44 or 50. Course is equivalent to SPAN101  CM and SPAN101  SC.

course.title: Spanglish in Context
course.description: What, exactly is "Spanglish," and who has the right to use it? How does this designation serve individuals as both a means of suppression and a practice of resistance? In this course we will investigate Spanish-English bilingualism in the U.S., focusing on empirical data from multiple theoretical perspectives: sociolinguistic, anthropological, political and literary. Prerequisite: SPAN 101 PO.

course.title: Intro to Technical Theatre
course.description: This course aims to provide a strong foundation in a variety of areas of theatre production. It emphasizes the technical departments of scenic, lighting, and sound as well as theatrical structures and areas of management. Students will gain practical skills in construction, and exposure to theatrical technologies, programs, and equipment utilized. Production lab and /or production crewing required.

course.title: Sound Design
course.description: This course introduces students to the process of creating artistically appropriate sound for theatre, and related forms of performance. Once mastery of sound equipment such as Q-Lab and Pro Tools is achieved, students will explore the artistic use of sound through a variety of dynamic hands-on creative projects. This project work is supplemented by reading, discussion and play attendance. May be repeated once for credit.

course.title: Acting Studio: Performing Comedy
course.description: Students will study the dynamic, precise, and often chaotic tools of comedy technique. In the first half of the semester, students will train in the tools of high comedy performance, paired with meticulously structured, witty farces (e.g. Wilde, Moliere, Ludwig, Frayn, Ayckbourn). In the second half of the semester, students will structure and create their own comedic content via stand-up (to be performed in public at open mics), sketch, and lazzi. Prerequisites: any THEA001 course and THEA 012 PO.

course.title: Autonomous Technology: AI Future
course.description: Is technology something we control, or something that increasingly controls us? This course examines that question as it has been posed by historians, philosophers, and critics of technology, focusing on the period since the 1960s. The course takes its title from Langdon Winner's _Autonomous Technology: Technics-out-of-Control as a Theme in Political Thought_ (1977). We read Winner alongside the two thinkers who most shaped the debate on either side of him: Jacques Ellul, who argued that "technique" had become a self-augmenting force beyond human direction, and Thomas P. Hughes, who showed how large technological systems acquire "momentum" while remaining human-built and contingent. Around this core I place Marx, Mumford, Heidegger, the technological determinism debate, the social construction of technology, and recent work on algorithms, automation, and AI.

course.title: Mommy Issues
course.description:
"Fathers loom large in the history of political thought. Since antiquity, the father's rule over the household has been the paradigmatic figure for naturalizing political authority. When English political philosopher and "father of liberalism," John Locke, rejected the divine right of kings and asserted the natural freedom and equality of men, he "killed" the political father. 

Mothers are more ambiguous figures in political theory. The figure of the mother is variously (and paradoxically) imagined as a natural site of childhood dominion, a passive subject of patriarchal rule, and a metaphor for the nation ("motherland," "mother tongue"). Feminist democratic theorists have sometimes turned to the "materna" as a symbol for pacifism, ethical commitment to the vulnerable, and compassionate civic values. By contrast, psychoanalysis (and popular culture) have often emphasized the pathological mother: possessive, overbearing, inappropriately sexual, manipulative, and ambivalent. 

What perhaps unites these divergent accounts is that the figure of the mother serves as a short-hand for forms of dependence and determinacy (biological, cultural, historical, linguistic, psycho-social, political) that frustrate liberal conceptions of the autonomous, self-making subject. If patricide liberates the liberal subject from the fatherâ¬"s law, does it also liberate her from the conditioning dependence that the figure of the mother represents? Of, if liberalism begins when free and equal sons and brothers birth themselves as a people, does this suggest, as Gil Anidjar (2024) has recently argued, that political action, rather than merely patricidal, is also primordially maternal? 

In this class, we will consider the gendered (and thus, raced and classed) figures and metaphors that structure conceptions of freedom and political subjectivity in liberal democracy. We will ask: what does it mean to be free? How can one be a self-making individual, while also being a "creature" of the body, of a family, and of a society? What is the relationship between freedom and dependence? Between individual will and fate? Does autonomy require isolation? Does freedom mean being without a history? Can the free subject both be sovereign, and also someone else's child?

course.title: Black Feminist Theory
course.description:
The United States Declaration of Independence famously declares that 'all men are created equal.' Bracketing, for the moment, the question of women's equality, this statement asserts the essential dignity and worth of each person. It also is an example of the passive voice. 

The black feminist poet and essayist, June Jordan, argued for eliminating the passive voice - the 'language of the powerful' - from our democracy. For Jordan, the passive voice masks the productive power of language, and displaces responsibility for the world(s) that our words create. Did Jordan have the Declaration of Independence in mind when she wrote these words? 

In contemporary multi-racial democracy, after the disappointments of the Civil Rights Movement and the "death of God" (Fredrich Nietzsche's description for the loss of faith in traditional authorities and absolute truths in modern life), Jordan invites us to ask: created equal - by whom?

In this class, we will consider the raced and gendered politics of language. We will begin by reading a selection of texts from a tradition of political thought known as social contract theory. At its best, social contract theory abstracts from the particular in order to give us general principles- like freedom and equality - to guide our shared political life. Black feminist theory offers a critical perspective on that promise. Thinkers such as Anna Julia Cooper, Audre Lorde, Hortense Spillers, and Toni Morrison draw from experiences of unfreedom and inequality to consider how (what Spillers calls) the "American grammar book" both shapes and constrains our ability to reimagine our shared political life. Working within and against the language and concepts of their inheritance, the black feminist theorists we will read in this class invite us to ask: how might we make political theory's abstract ideals concrete?

course.title: Queer Histories in the US
course.description: Focusing on the twentieth century U.S., this course explores the historical experiences of people we might today consider lesbian, bisexual, gay, trans, and queer (LGBTQ+). We will examine how these communitiesâ¬ and the identity categories that define themâ¬were shaped by complex economic, cultural, and legal factors. Topics include the medicalization of homosexuality and gender variance, urbanization, nightlife, labor, state persecution, queer migrations, liberation movements, HIV/AIDS, and the influence of race and class on sexual/gender identity and community formation. The course will provide critical historical context for contemporary societal anxieties about same-sex marriage, drag, and transition-related healthcare.

course.title: Living History/Digital Archives
course.description: This course is your chance to help shape Pitzer's institutional memory through the creation of digital archives that tell community stories. We will discuss the theory and meaning of the 'archive,' interrogate some of its many forms, and examine how it contributes to shaping institutional, cultural, and community memory. Some of the questions we will examine include: What does it mean to create an inclusive archival memory? How can we balance accessibility with privacy? What does ethical digital archives work look like in the age of AI? This project-based seminar will be centered on the creation of a digital archives project. You will learn how to work with an organization on meeting its needs and fulfilling its vision while engaging and applying best practices for archival work. Our community partnership will focus on Pitzer College and its history.

course.title: Intro to Editing and Publishing
course.description: Have you ever been curious about what it would be like to not only publish in, but edit an academic journal?  In this course, we will plan and produce a student-run research journal to serve as an academic publication site at Pitzer College. Through an evaluation of current best practices for scholarly publishing, we will address topics such as our goals and purposes in publishing a research journal, inclusive selection practices and avoiding publication bias, peer review and editing processes, the difference between reviewers and editors, the implications of AI for submission evaluation, and developing an interdisciplinary approach. On the publication side, we will design peer review processes and digital publishing options and consider future directions for the journal and its role in advancing student-driven research among Pitzer students. Plus, your name will feature on the masthead of the final publication as an associate editor!

course.title: Gender, Sexuality, Power: S Asia
course.description:
"In this class, we examine how gender, sexuality, and power are produced, lived, and contested across South Asia. Rather than treating the region as a peripheral case, the course approaches South Asia as a site of feminist and queer theory-making, political imagination, and world-building in its own right. We ask how histories of caste, colonial governance, religion, nationalism, and development have shaped gendered and sexualized lives, and how these formations are reworked through activism, ethical practice, and everyday survival. Ethnographic works anchor the course, complemented by fiction and documentary films and conversations with activists working in the region. Through these forms of engagement, students will encounter diverse feminist and queer identities, movements, and intellectual traditions while examining how broader historical and political forces take shape in everyday relationships, embodied practices, and moral worlds. Students will learn to approach feminism and queerness not as fixed categories but as analytic tools forged through struggle and debate, capable of unsettling binaries, hierarchies, and normative assumptions. The course equips students to bring anthropological approaches into conversation with interdisciplinary feminist and queer scholarship to analyze global debates about gender, sexuality, rights, development, migration, and media from perspectives grounded in South Asia. No prior background in South Asia or gender studies is required.

The class opens by situating gender and sexuality within South Asiaâ¬"s longer histories of caste, religion, colonialism, and nationalism, establishing a shared vocabulary for thinking about power and difference. We then examine colonial debates over women, sexuality, and social reform before turning to womenâ¬"s movements forged through intertwined struggles over labor, law, and state repression. From there, the course traces how gender and sexuality have been regulated, contested, and lived across changing political contexts, including through queer and trans communitiesâ¬" struggles over recognition and belonging. As the semester progresses, we analyze how projects of development, reform, nationalism, and religious politics reorganize intimate life and moral authority, and how caste, class, and affect shape the making of modern subjects. The course concludes with attention to media, diaspora, and transnational formations, highlighting feminist and queer futures that cross borders, reimagine belonging, and critique power."

course.title: Philosophy in Claremont
course.description: This course introduces students to philosophical research at the Claremont Colleges through a team-taught format. Approximately six philosophy faculty members from across the five colleges present work drawn from their published scholarship as well as ongoing projects. Topics span major areas of philosophy and its history, including Metaphysics, Philosophy of Science, Philosophy of Mind, Epistemology, and Ethics. Each presentation is preceded by an introductory session that provides the conceptual background necessary for engagement. By integrating foundational instruction with direct exposure to faculty research, the course offers both a broad overview of philosophy and insight into how philosophical inquiry is practiced within the Claremont community.

course.title: Environmental Justice in the IE
course.description: What is environmental justice, and how do historical, political, economic, and social processes shape the environments where people live and work? This course examines environmental justice through the landscapes, communities, and histories of Southern California's Inland Empire. Drawing on interdisciplinary approaches from the social sciences, environmental studies, and the humanities, we examine how race, class, labor, colonialism, gender, and political power shape environmental conditions and produce unequal experiences of environmental harm and protection. Students will engage with foundational debates in environmental justice, environmental racism, and political ecology to understand how these processes operate within and beyond the region. Throughout the semester, we will examine environmental justice issues in the Inland Empire, including warehousing and logistics, agricultural labor, pollution, land use, water, and environmental organizing. Through these case studies, students will explore how historical and contemporary power relations shape the region's landscapes, communities, and environmental conditions. We will also consider how environmental issues in the Inland Empire connect to larger regional, national, and global systems and processes.
