Through these case studies, students will explore how historical and contemporary power relations shape the region's landscapes, communities, and environmental conditions. We will also consider how environmental issues in the Inland Empire connect to larger regional, national, and global systems and processes.

course.title: Reality TV
course.description: This course will critically examine reality television in the global media industries.  Taking a historical approach, it will consider the pre-history of reality television through its rise in the early 2000s into the present day.   Using reality TV history as a frame, this course will examine the changing role of labor, media conglomeratization and platformization, new media technologies, and globalization within media industries.

course.title: Critical AI: Justice, Labor, and
course.description:
"'AI will probably...lead to the end of the world," Sam Altman said in 2015," but in the meantime, there'll be great companies." AI doomerism and boosterism both depend on what Raley and Rhee (2023) call "performative wonder." By representing AI as an inscrutable black box or oracle, they foreclose rigorous debate about real world harms and histories (Goodlad 2023). This seminar is grounded in critical AI studies, an emergent field that builds technical, sociocultural, and historical literacies in order to hold these technologies, and those who build them, accountable to the public interest.

Organized around the Munroe Center for Social Inquiry's public lecture series, the seminar asks: how do AI systems reproduce inequalities? Who benefits from AI's accelerating development, and who absorbs its social, environmental, and labor costs? How might the arts and community organizing help us critique, resist, and reimagine technological futures? Speakers include Pulitzer Prize-winning poet Juliana Spahr; Gugenheim fellow Allison Pugh, Turkopticon co-founder Lilly Irani, and Hamid Khan of the Stop LAPD Spying Coalition, among others. You will read the work of roughly a dozen invited speakers and create a public podcast based on the talks and your own interviews with scholars, activists, and artists."

course.title: Senior Thesis Seminar
course.description: The EA Senior Thesis Seminar is required for ALL EA majors doing a thesis who are not already enrolled in another thesis seminar. In this course, students will work intensively in developing, researching and writing their semester-long theses. Students will also engage in peer editing and professional presentation of their research.

course.title: Senior Thesis
course.description:
Students who choose to write a senior thesis must present a
proposal or paper to the Political Studies/Economics Field Group at the end of the
prior semester for approval. Students will work closely with their faculty thesis
advisers. Prerequisites: a senior seminar in Political Studies and field group
approval. Staff.

course.title: Communicating Black Risk
course.description: A polluted river is a physical reality, but it does not speak for itself. Whether environmental pollution, public health disparities, state violence, or climate change become recognized as crises depends, in part, on communication: Who speaks? Who is heard? Who is believed? Communicating Black Risk examines how media and public discourse shape understandings of risks affecting Black communities across Africa and the African diaspora. Drawing on scholarship in communication, media studies, environmental justice, public health, and critical race theory, we will investigate how public narratives influence what societies recognize as matters of public concern. Through historical and contemporary case studies, we will develop a critical understanding of the dual power of communication: its capacity to render risks visible or invisible, legitimize or dismiss lived experiences, and reinforce or challenge existing inequalities.

course.title: Toxic Ground, Fertile Ground
course.description: In this course, we investigate how societies understand, shape, and relate to nature. Drawing on core concepts on the social construction of nature, the political economy of resource use, and environmental justice, we analyze how societies produce, value, and contest environmental knowledge. Through case studies across Indigenous communities, the African diaspora, Latin America, and the broader Global South, we also trace how colonial histories, resource extraction, climate change, and environmental inequalities transform relationships between communities and the environment. At the same time, we examine how communities cultivate fertile ground - just and sustainable environmental futures fueled by diverse forms of knowledge, reimagined relationships and collective action

course.title: Global to Local Comm, Edu, Rsrch
course.description: This course bridges local and global perspectives on core values, ethical frameworks, and critical approaches for building reciprocal relationships with communities, supporting students looking for meaningful academic experiences at home and abroad that engage with local communities working for social change. The course includes workshops with local community partners, panels with experts in the field, (including alumni), and student-taught lesson plans, thus allowing students to engage with real-world examples of social justice work, education, arts, and cultural exchange that occur through Pitzerâ¬"s community partnerships both locally and across our global partnerships. Students will learn more about and introduce direct involvement with Pitzerâ¬"s local community engagement programs and study abroad programs. The Spring 2027 course will have a special focus on Brazilian arts and culture, including capoeira, dance, and drumming alongside theater of the oppressed frameworks as part of the study of how local and abroad communities advance community-building and social change through traditional arts and culture. All students completing this course will be eligible to apply for IGLAS funding for a project or internship while studying abroad, and/or for an opportunity to join a faculty-led site visit to a Pitzer program in Brazil in the summer.

course.title: First-Year Humanities Seminar
course.description: The Freshman Humanities Seminar (FHS) program aims to give first-year students an introduction to some of the questions fundamental to individuals in their relationship to society and the world. Each section engages one or more critical themes such as the notion of the self, the community, individual and communal values, modes of understanding, and creative expression, and the relationships each one has with the others. In doing so, all FHS courses include historically significant texts: texts that have become objects of academic discourse in part because of their enormous impact in non-academic contexts.

course.title: First-Year Humanities Seminar

Each section engages one or more critical themes such as the notion of the self, the community, individual and communal values, modes of understanding, and creative expression, and the relationships each one has with the others. In doing so, all FHS courses include historically significant texts: texts that have become objects of academic discourse in part because of their enormous impact in non-academic contexts.

course.title: Specl Topcs Cermcs: Casting&Nat
course.description: In this introductory sculptural ceramics course, we will explore the genre of ecological art practice through a series of engaged learning projects. We will conduct interdisciplinary research, field collection, and work collaboratively to develop ceramic projects. Ceramic topics covered will include hand-building techniques, paper clay preparation, sustainable collection methods, organic burnout, surface and color, and firing and non-firing finish options. Course meets Fine Arts general education requirement.

course.title: 3D Modeling and Animation
course.description: This interdisciplinary intermediate course examines the history, theory, and techniques of 3D modeling and animation. Through exercises, critical readings, and projects, students will engage with 3D software as a technical tool, artistic medium, and cultural object. This course introduces foundational skills in modeling, rendering, and animation using various software. Course meets Fine Arts general education requirement.

course.title: Advanced Fiction Writing
course.description: This advanced fiction workshop is intended for people who have taken at least one semester of Fiction Writing (Lit. 38).  Each student will submit two stories or novel excerpts for workshop, where they will be carefully critiqued by the class.  We'll also read short fiction by well-known contemporary writers, with an eye toward what makes these stories original, entertaining, and complex.  In class, we'll look beyond basic elements of craft and address issues of concern for the experienced writer.  How do we avoid cliche?  Create narrative drive?  Take risks with form, language, and subject matter? Written exercises will focus on these issues while challenging students to push their writing in unexpected directions. May be repeated once for credit. May count toward the CMC literature major only once. Prerequisite: LIT 038 CM.

course.title: Arts of Late Imperial China
course.description: This course will examine the arts of late imperial China during the Ming (1368-1644) and Qing (1644-1911) dynasties. How did the literati elite engage with the classical painting tradition and respond to dynastic change? How did the imperial court in Beijing cultivate cosmopolitan tastes? How was China inextricably connected to global trade and empire building? This course will include opportunities to learn directly from artworks in the teaching collections at The Claremont Colleges. Course meets Letters general education requirement.

course.title: Intermediate Latin
course.description: For students with two or three years of secondary school Latin or one year of college Latin. Selections from Latin poetry and prose of the late Republic and early Empire. Reading and translation from texts; grammar review and composition. Prerequisites: LATN001, LATN002, LATN022.

course.title: Lemme Cook: Art of Food Writing
course.description:
investigative journalism, to the sheer pleasures of food as a space in which community is forged and memory cemented. In this course, students will have the opportunity to investigate forms and techniques of food writing across the field and generate their
own. Writers who move deftly between genres will be read such as: Rebecca May Johnson, Ruby Tandoh, Mark Arax, Rachel Signer, Francesca Ekwuyasi, Ruth Reichl, and Bryant Terry.

course.title: Prose Style & the Sentence
course.description: This is a course about sentences. We will study how to appreciate and analyze them; how to expand and contract them; how to translate them from one register/style to another; and how to move their words around for rhetorical effect. We will read from a few style handbooks (with exercises), scrutinize sentences from a wide range of sources, imitate some major stylists, compose a couple of short papers, and even try our hand at diagramming sentences, as well as complete a course project. Mostly, though, we will take a workshop approach to crafting a wide range of sentences in which every word tells.

course.title: Interpreting Religious Worlds
course.description: Required of all majors and minors. Examines some current approaches to the study of religion as a legitimate field of academic discourse. This course is taught in alternating years at Scripps, Pomona, and Claremont McKenna Colleges.

course.title: Introduction to Sociology
course.description: This course examines introductory concepts and theories in the study of Sociology. Attention is given to sociological theory, inequality of race, class, gender, and sexuality, white privilege, as well as power, authority, and movements for social change.

course.title: Queer Art, Literature and Visual
course.description: This course offers a reflection on key art and literary practices and fundamental theories which develop an understanding of queerness. Stepping away from â¬Üqueerâ¬" as an identity marker, the readings and work offered will articulate how queer operates as a verb to subvert or wholly turn away from conventional understandings of life to cultivate radical alternatives. Each week a theoretical text is paired with a â¬Ücase studyâ¬" to offer an opening conversation on the political implications of queering art and literature. The course will oscillate between texts in the mediums of art, visual culture, performance, and literature to understand how queerness challenges and subverts the normative conventions of form and gender/genre, as well as challenging the normative conventions that structure life under colonial capitalism.

course.title: Queer of Color Critique
course.description: Queer of Color Critique (QoCC) derives from Roderick Ferguson?s seminal Aberrations in Black: Toward a Queer of Color Critique. Ferguson?s framework and the resulting interdisciplinary field of Queer of Color Critique is rooted in women of color feminism, queer studies, and materialist analysis. This course familiarizes students with the cultural, political, and economic concerns of QoCC, and how it interrupts socially dominant categories of sexuality, including the implicitly white and masculine subject of queer theory. Through QoCC the course explores the political and ethical necessity of carving out space for desires, attachments, and modes of relation which are not always legible or are considered taboo. One of the primary goals of the course is to explore several keywords ? such as queer, desire, future, and sexuality ? through interrogations of the prison-industrial complex, the police state, and economic restructuring. Completing 1 prior course in GFS/FGSS/GWS is a prerequisite for enrolling in this course.

course.title: Science and Religion
course.description:
Taking a comparative and interdisciplinary approach - drawing from history, sociology, and secular studies - this class examines religion and science. What are they? What is their relationship to each other? How have they been socially constructed over time? How have science and religion alternately conflicted, collaborated, and mutually influenced one another? 
Course will entail some lecture, some debate, and plenty of discussion. Screens will not be permitted.

course.title: Finding Gaza
course.description: How can we draw inspiration from the rich arts, culture, and history of the Gaza Strip to craft poetry? Focusing on the ongoing siege and genocide, students will explore how to transform news content, historical narratives, and the resilience of Gaza's people into powerful poems. Through analysis of Gaza's current events and artistic traditions in the broader context of Palestine and the Arab World, students will learn to capture moments of struggle, hope, and resistance in their work, using poetry as a medium for storytelling, activism, and personal reflection. Students will develop skills to create emotionally resonant poems and workshop them together, as well as interview and have conversations with Gazan artists and write about them.

course.title: QF Science & Technology Studies
course.description: How do human biases creep into scientific structures, processes, and discourses, despite aspirations toward empiricism? This course takes interest in how social ideas around gender and sexuality have been informed by and contribute to emerging studies in endocrinology, quantum physics, and cognitive science, as well as developments in mathematics, computation, and statistical science. In addition to covering histories of exclusion from STEM fields, the course offers tools from critical disability studies and critical race theory to address histories of eugenicist thought as well as notions of social improvement and hierarchical taxonomies that have supported discriminatory practices and outright violence. Part historical and part theoretical, we will ultimately examine contemporary pressures on both science and gender and sexuality studies as authoritative sites of knowledge production.

course.title: Sociology of Religion
course.description: An exploration of the collective dynamics of religious life, encompassing interaction, meaning, culture, organizational behavior, new religious movements, and the mediatization of spirituality.

course.title: Feminism and Science (CP)
course.description: This course examines feminist perspectives on and critiques of science and technology, traditional scientific world views, and how gendered and other values inform scientific theory and practice. Topics include the current and historical participation of women in science, with attention to race, class, and nationality; scientific theories of sex differences; the scientific construction of sex; issues in women's health; and environmental issues. This is a Napier course and will include participation of several elder co-learners from the Pilgrim Place retirement community, offering an opportunity for intergenerational discussion, mentoring and projects.  Students will also participate in several Tuesday evening writing group sessions at the local state women's prison.

course.title: Indigenous Ecologies
course.description: This course will introduce students to the history and futures of Indigenous Ecologies.  We will critically engage with concepts such as settler colonialism and coloniality to understand how environments have been transformed and altered at times to a point beyond repair. Moving beyond a damage-centered approach, we will focus on Traditional Ecological Knowledge and Indigenous resistance thinking through struggles for water, land, fire, and air. The course weaves stories from Tongva Land and AbyaYala (the Americas), taking a hemispheric approach to indigeneity and ecology. Particular attention will be given to the intersections of race, class, gender, and sexuality to understand the nuanced relationships Indigenous people have with the environment. We will also examine Indigenous cultural productions such as films, literature, and zines to consider the types of futures that are made possible by radically reorienting our relationships with the ecologies we are from or guests on.

course.title: Intro African American Psych
course.description: Situating the study of human development in the context of culture has gained tremendous momentum over the past few decades. This course is designed to examine theoretical and empirical issues relating to the psychology of African Americans. Specific attention will be given to (1) traditional and africentric approaches to the study of African American Psychology, (2) issues of measurement of the minority personality (testing bias, intelligence testing etc), and (3) individual and developmental issues, such as cognition, self-concept, self-esteem and racial identity. This course begins with an overview African American Psychology as an evolving field of study and considers the African American paradigm as one of the key conceptual frameworks for understanding the psychological experiences of African Americans.

course.title: Spring Senior Seminar
course.description: Senior Seminar. Jointly-taught seminar designed for senior majors. Review of key issues/theories in media studies.

course.title: Claremont Treble Singers
course.description: A study through rehearsal and performance of choral music for soprano and alto voices selected from the 14th century to the present. Singers will be invited to register after a successful audition. Singers continuing from the previous semester need not audition.

course.title: Intro to Data Science with R
course.description: This course will introduce students to the foundations of data science using environmental and social applications. Using the R programming language, we will learn data gathering and cleaning, visualization, network analysis, modeling, visualization, ethics, and interpretation. Students will develop projects in which they implement the full data science pipeline, from idea generation to results and interpretations.

course.title: 1-Semester Sr Thesis Dual Mjr
course.description:
Scripps Senior Thesis for Dual Majors, one semester thesis. If you will complete a one-semester Senior Thesis for your dual major, register for this course. You must also complete a Senior Thesis Registration Form by the add deadline of the semseter in which you complete your thesis. Once submitted, the Registrar's Office will update your thesis registration to reflect a section with your readers listed as instructors. Contact your readers to understand the expectations of your senior thesis, and agree upon a deadline amenable to both majors. 

More information regarding thesis can be found on the Inside Registrar page: https://inside.scrippscollege.edu/registrar/student-resources/graduating-seniors/senior-thesis

course.title: International Economics
course.description: A survey of topics in international trade and finance. Included are studies of the law of comparative advantage, patterns of trade between nations, and the financial relationships involved in transactions in international markets. The course also examines the motivation and form of government policies which influence international flows of money and goods. Prerequisites: Economics 52 and 102, or permission from instructor.

course.title: Senior Thesis in History
course.description: Fall enrollment for a one-semester thesis, or a two-semester thesis. Enroll for HIST192 SC in the spring for a two-semester thesis.

course.title: Development of American Markets
course.description: The economic history of the United States is one of the extension of markets over a vast geographical space. This course will examine both input and output markets in the 200 years after the American Revolution. How did those markets first form and how did they evolve over time? When were they efficient, and when did they fail? How was the pace and pattern of growth affected? Prerequisites: Economics 51 and 52.

course.title: Senior Thesis
Senior Thesis in Art History
Sr Thesis: Ancient St/Classics
course.description: Students will work closely and on an individual basis with their faculty advisers to identify an area of interest, become familiar with basic bibliography and research tools, and define a topic to investigate. Students will submit the results of this research in writing and make an oral presentation to the Ancient Studies/Classics Department. Restricted to seniors majoring in Classics.

course.title: Senior Thesis in English
course.description: Scripps senior English majors who are taking one of the seminars eligible for the senior requirement (course number ending in S) are concurrently enrolled in this course as well. ENGL199T SC refers to the 30-page thesis that emerges from those seminars. Fall or spring, depending on the senior seminar. Formerly ENGL191

course.title: Sr Thesis: Fem Gndr Sex Studies
course.description: Thesis is an original investigation on a topic in Feminist, Gender, and Sexuality Studies within the discipline of concentration, completed under the guidance of the reader in the department of concentration and a reader in the Scripps Department of Feminist, Gender, and Sexuality Studies.

course.title: Senior Thesis in French Studies
course.description: The culmination of a student's French major, the thesis requires her to think creatively, analytically, and critically about a topic of her choice in consultation with the French faculty. Students propose their topic at an early fall thesis meeting and present a minimum of their first chapter upon return from winter recess. Whereas regular theses are generally 10,000 to 15,000 words (40-70 pages double-spaced), honors thesis are approximately 17,000 to 25,000 words (75-100 pages double-spaced). Senior theses are written in French. If a student is a dual major, the requirement to write in French may be waived with permission of the Scripps French Department.

course.title: Senior Thesis in History
course.description: Spring enrollment for a two-semester thesis; enroll in HIST191 SC for the fall semester.

course.title: Sr Thesis: Humanities Major
course.description: Fall enrollment for a one-semester thesis, or a two-semester thesis. Enroll for HMSC192 SC in the spring for a two-semester thesis.

course.title: Senior Thesis: Religious Studies
course.description: Required of all senior majors in Religious Studies.

course.title: Anthropology of Care
course.description: This course explores anthropological perspectives on care, centering ethnographic accounts of care practices globally to understand the economic, political, moral, and lived realities of care. Throughout the course we will look at how care has been theorized within medical anthropology and healthcare settings, feminist critiques of care as a moral practice, care in relation to kinship and relatedness, and the economization of care and care work.

course.title: Nourishing Life
course.description: "Nourishing Life" translates yangshen, a phrase early Chinese thinkers coined in their debates on how to best care for oneself. The techniques, spanning from dietary and hygiene observances, physical exercises, alchemy, to moral conduct and mental training, often seek to harmonize body and mind, as well as the cosmos. The arts of nourishing life are also elaborated in later Buddhist, Confucian, and Daoist literature, as well as in East Asian writings. Through close readings of selected primary sources in English translation (e.g. Mencius, Zhuangzi, Dogen's "Instruction to the Cook," and a Tibetan tantric meditation manual), we will analyze the different recipes proposed by East Asian thinkers for prolonging life and attaining health, and the different biological, ethical, philosophical, psychological, and at times spiritual assumptions undergirding their concepts of health and wellbeing.

course.title: General Chemistry w/Laboratory
course.description: General Chemistry with Lab. An introduction to the theories exploring the physical and chemical properties of the elements and their compounds, including the structure and properties of solids, liquids and gases. Topics include nuclear chemistry, quantum theory, atomic and molecular structure via orbital theory, chemical bonding, coordination chemistry, spectroscopy, chemical kinetics and the properties of multicomponent solutions and electrolytes. Laboratory work is coordinated with the lecture and emphasizes quantitative analytical and instrumental techniques. Pre-requisite: CHEM 010A PO.

course.title: The Novels of Vladimir Nabokov
course.description: Emphasis on Nabokovs cultivation of his reader, metafiction and the role of cross-cultural experience in literary creativity. Equal time spent on Russian and American periods. Texts include The Defense; Lolita; Pale Fire. All readings in English. (Russian in Translation)

course.title: Critical Analysis Through Lit
course.description:
Critical Analysis Though Literature


Short stories, essays and novels exploring a range of American experiences will provide a basis for students to develop an understanding of the social, political, historical and philosophical thought that informs this literature and the language needed to express an analysis of these works. Students must enroll in the corresponding First-Year Seminar (MLLC 133). Letter grades only. Written permission required.

course.title: Community-engaged Design
course.description:
Community-engaged Design for a more Just Public Realm
The discipline of urban planning has vast social, economic, environmental, and health-related impact on the lives of people across the city. All too often, though, this impact has been delivered unequally, along the familiar lines of race, class, and gender. This course sets out to establish tenets of urban planning that focus squarely on justice and that create equity in the built environment. In it, we will examine urban public spaces in Southern California through the lenses of homelessness, gender equity, and racial justice. We will use a participatory planning approach to reimagine these spaces with designs that incorporate the voices of diverse communities historically ignored during park creation.

course.title: Fascism: Politics and Histories
course.description:
Crosslisted with POST153  PZ

What is fascism? What are its origins? What are its practices? How do we know it when we see it?  What have been the political and social responses to it?  To explore these questions, this seminar considers the emergence, florescence, and limits  of fascism in 20th century Europe, particularly in Italy, Spain, and Germany. In doing so, it also considers fascismâ¬"s reception in the United States.

course.title: Introduction to Psychology
course.description: The purpose of the course is to introduce the student to psychology as it developed from a nonscientific interest to a scientific approach to human behavior. Special attention will be given to some of the major systems, issues and methods involved in contemporary psychology. Students will be expected to participate in research studies in psychology or complete an approved alternative.

course.title: Psychological Disorders
course.description: This course provides a broad overview to psychopathology and the study of psychological disorders, including depressive, anxiety, addictive, somatic, eating, psychotic, and personality disorders. Topics include" Theoretical perspectives for conceptualizing "normal" and "abnormal" behavior; approaches to defining, assessing and treating major symptom domains; and critical evaluation of current research on the causes and mechanisms of mental illness.

course.title: Design, Comp. & Human Experience
course.description: This course examines computing as a form of design and human-computer interaction as a historical, philosophical, and cultural phenomenon. Rather than treating interfaces as neutral tools or HCI as a collection of design techniques, we will look at how computers have reshaped ideas about thought, action, communication, embodiment, work, and everyday life, as well as how those things have reshaped how we think of computing.

course.title: Pop Culture & the Pacific Island
course.description: This course critically examines the relationship between popular culture and the Pacific Islands. Using concepts and theories in cultural studies, history, Indigenous studies, and media studies, students will learn how to analyze aesthetics, form, historical context, meaning, power, and representation embedded in popular culture. Some of the various forms of popular culture that will be explored include fashion, films, graphic novels, music, sports, and television. Additionally, emphasis will be placed on intersecting themes such as capitalism, gender, indigeneity, racism, and settler colonialism.

course.title: Continental Thought
course.description: Continental Thought. Beginning with a review of Kant, German idealism (Fichte through Hegel), Kierkegaard, Schopenhauer, Nietzsche, Heidegger, Foucault and Derrida will be considered.

course.title: Devising Theatre
course.description: This course is open to live performance practitioners of all kinds: actors, singers, dancers, musicians, performance artists, video artists, designers, and technicians. Participants will engage with a performance-based approach to devising (creating) live performance. Solo and group performances may be inspired by a variety of forms and content, including interviews, archival materials, visual art, music, and other texts or movement scores. Students will come away with tools for both solo and collaborative creation. We will primarily use in-class time to build skills, collaborate, and rehearse. Work created in class may be performed publicly on campus at the end of the semester.

course.title: Contemporary Performance Praxis
course.description: The goal of this course is to help prepare students for senior projects and professional work. This course provides a foundation in four main categories: Building ethical and equitable theatre-making processes; professional growth and skill-building; community development; and creating personalized methodologies and goals for future theatrical endeavors. We will hold workshops to expand our professional toolkit, adventure on a community-building outing, and deepen our ever-evolving understanding of ethical and equitable practices. Students will formulate their own aesthetic, philosophical, and critical points of view about theatre. Presentations, reflection papers, and weekly discussion will lead towards the final project: a senior project proposal, delivered to the full faculty and staff of the theatre department.

course.title: We Shoot Back
course.description: The objective of this course is to examine the histories and historiographies of the rebellions and revolts of the enslaved.  This seminar will introduce students to the methods and questions of modern history through an exploration of the theories and praxis of insurgent actions the enslaved undertook to re-make their lives and the lives of others during the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.  Real and imagined, these events shaped the development and eventual collapse of slavery in the (so called) ?New World.?  Assigned readings consist of historical texts and autobiographies.  Seminars will contextualize the readings by placing the authors in history and addressing their significance.  Throughout the course, we will explore the possibilities that violent Black rebellion opens (and forecloses) with an eye towards our current historical moment.

course.title: Puppet Design
course.description: In this introductory course, students will study puppetry design, performance, and production. Using hands-on techniques, students will learn fabrication, media techniques, and puppetry manipulation to create their own puppets.

course.title: Queer Art, Literature and Visual
course.description: This course offers a reflection on key art and literary practices and fundamental theories which develop an understanding of queerness. Stepping away from 'queer' as an identity marker, the readings and work offered will articulate how queer operates as a verb to subvert or wholly turn away from conventional understandings of life to cultivate radical alternatives. Each week a theoretical text is paired with a 'case study' to offer an opening conversation on the political implications of queering art and literature. The course will oscillate between texts in the mediums of art, visual culture, performance, and literature to understand how queerness challenges and subverts the normative conventions of form and gender/genre, as well as challenging the normative conventions that structure life under colonial capitalism.

course.title: Art and Aesthetics
course.description: The course will focus on issues concerning the nature of art and its value. Issues include the role of interpretation in determining the meaning of artworks; the question of whether forgery that is visually identical to an original work has less aestheticvalue and if so, why; and problems arising from certain kinds of artworks, like why we have emotional responses to fictional characters and whether it is rational to do so.

course.title: Futurecraft
course.description: In this course, we will theorize Futurecraft as the act of building futures under conditions of constraint (political, social, or otherwise) through acts of creation using the tools at hand (our words, technology, and our imagination). We will read how writers and thinkers from across the twentieth and twenty-first centuries have understood and attempted to shape the future through genres like utopian and dystopian fiction, political and artist manifestos, and zines as well as through the digital rhetorics of new media platforms and online activism. We will explore these genres and rhetorics through analytical and creative writing assignments.

course.title: Global Social Movements
course.description: Social movements today are inherently global, networked, and diffused. This course examines the possibilities and limitations of global movements in the 21st century. The course introduces classic social movement theory and concepts, explores their applications in a globalized world, and surveys the contemporary landscape of mobilization across all regions of the world.

course.title: Individual Instruction, Level I
course.description: Individual Instruction, Level I. Half-hour lesson weekly.

course.title: Individual Instruction, Level I+
course.description: Individual Instruction, Level I+. Half-hour lesson weekly.

course.title: Individual Instruction, Level II
course.description: Individual Instruction, Level II. Initial enrollment is dependent upon successful completion of a qualifying examination. 20: half-hour lesson weekly, cumulative credit, each semester; 100: hour lesson weekly, half-course, each semester. Satisfactory grades required for continued study. More information is available from the Music Department.

course.title: Individual Instruction, Level II
course.description: Individual Instruction, Level II. Initial enrollment is dependent upon successful completion of a qualifying examination. 20: half-hour lesson weekly, cumulative credit, each semester; 100: hour lesson weekly, half-course, each semester. Satisfactory grades required for continued study. More information is available from the Music Department secretary.

course.title: Health & Health Care Costa Rica
course.description: Students who plan to participate in the Costa Rica Summer Health Program are required to take this course during the spring semester immediately before their program. The seminar covers an introduction to epidemiology and health care in Costa Rica as well as units on history, environment, economy, and politics, and a workshop on intercultural learning.  Students are required to learn how to understand and analyze various sources of population and public health data, write a series of four short papers, give an oral presentation with an accompanying background paper, and complete a series of exercises dealing with the kinds of intercultural challenges they will likely confront during their homestays and internships in Costa Rica.

course.title: Performing Art: Sexuality/Gender
course.description: Investigation of what it means to be man, woman, male, female, heterosexual, bisexual, homosexual, transgendered, non-conforming and non-binary individuals in contemporary American society through representations in the fine and performing arts. Special attention to ways in which the popular culture media shape the images of what is desirable and often stereotypical in gendered roles.

course.title: Science and Religion
course.description:
Taking a comparative and interdisciplinary approach - drawing from history, sociology, and secular studies - this class examines religion and science. What are they? What is their relationship to each other? How have they been socially constructed over time? How have science and religion alternately conflicted, collaborated, and mutually influenced one another? 
Course will entail some lecture, some debate, and plenty of discussion. Screens will not be permitted.

course.title: Empirical Methods
course.description:
This course introduces students to the philosophy and practice of political science research. Students will learn how to identify a problem worthy of study, develop testable hypotheses, design a research strategy, gather data, analyze data, and interpret and present the results. Topics covered include research design, descriptive statistics, data visualization, statistical inference, hypothesis testing, correlation, and regression analysis (cross-section, time-series, and panel data models).
Prerequisite: GOVT020  CM. Not available to students who have earned credit for any other course in statistics including: ECON120  CM, MATH052 CM, ECON125  CM, or PSYC109  CM.
